chapters.title: GST: Supply and Charge in Depth
chapters.summary: Scope of supply under section 7 and Schedules I to III, composite and mixed supply, the levy under section 9 CGST and section 5 IGST, reverse charge and the rate structure after the September 2025 rationalisation.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST and IGST Acts as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Scope of supply: section 7 and Schedules I to III
lesson.body:
Section 7(1) of the CGST Act makes **supply** the taxable event. It covers all forms of supply of goods or services (sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease, disposal) made or agreed to be made **for a consideration** by a person **in the course or furtherance of business**. It also covers import of services for consideration, whether or not in the course of business, and activities by a club or association to its members (section 7(1)(aa), inserted with effect from 1 July 2017).

**Schedule I** lists activities that are supply even **without consideration**:

- Permanent transfer or disposal of business assets where input tax credit (ITC) was availed on them.
- Supply between **related persons** or between **distinct persons** (section 25: separate registrations of the same PAN), in the course of business. Gifts by an employer to an employee up to ₹50,000 in a financial year are not supply.
- Supply of goods by a principal to an agent who supplies them on behalf of the principal, or by an agent to a principal who receives them on his behalf.
- Import of services from a related person or from his own establishment outside India, in the course of business.

**Schedule II** only classifies an activity as goods or services (for example, transfer of right to use goods is a service; works contract is a service; supply of food or drink as part of a service is a service).

**Schedule III** lists activities that are **neither** supply of goods nor services:

| Para | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment |
| 2 | Services by a court or tribunal |
| 3 | Functions of MPs, MLAs, members of local bodies; constitutional functionaries |
| 4 | Services of a funeral, burial, crematorium or mortuary |
| 5 | Sale of land and, subject to para 5 of Schedule II, sale of a building |
| 6 | Actionable claims, other than specified actionable claims (betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery, online money gaming) |
| 7 | Supply of goods from a place outside India to another place outside India without the goods entering India (merchant trade) |
| 8(a) | Sale of warehoused goods to any person before clearance for home consumption |
| 8(b) | High seas sale, by endorsement of documents of title, before clearance for home consumption |

lesson.heading: Composite and mixed supply (sections 2(30), 2(74) and 8)
lesson.body:
When two or more supplies are made together, section 8 decides the rate.

| Point | Composite supply | Mixed supply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Section 2(30) | Section 2(74) |
| Bundling | **Naturally bundled**, supplied together in the ordinary course of business | Not naturally bundled; combined by choice |
| Price | Usually one price, but separate prices do not by themselves break a natural bundle | **Single price** for the combination |
| Rate | Rate of the **principal supply** (section 2(90)) | **Highest rate** among the items |
| Example | Goods with packing, transport and insurance; a hotel room with breakfast | A Diwali hamper of sweets, dry fruits and an aerated drink |

Tests for natural bundling: the perception of the consumer, normal trade practice, whether the elements are advertised as one package and whether one element is merely ancillary to another.

A works contract (section 2(119)) and supply of food in a restaurant are treated as **services** by Schedule II, so you do not need the composite test for them.

**Worked example.** A dealer sells a gift box for ₹10,000 containing sweets (5%), a decorative steel bowl (18%) and an aerated beverage (40%). It is a mixed supply at a single price, so the entire ₹10,000 is taxed at 40%: GST ₹4,000. If the dealer had priced each item separately, each would carry its own rate.

lesson.heading: Charge: section 9 CGST, section 5 IGST and the post-September 2025 rates
lesson.body:
Section 9(1) CGST levies tax on all **intra-State** supplies (except alcoholic liquor for human consumption) on the value under section 15, at rates notified on the recommendation of the GST Council, not exceeding 20% (so CGST plus SGST is capped at 40%). Section 5(1) IGST levies tax on **inter-State** supplies and on imports, capped at 40%. IGST on imported goods is collected under the Customs Tariff Act at the customs frontier.

Five petroleum products (petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel) are within GST but taxable only from a date notified on the Council's recommendation (section 9(2)). Until then they bear central excise and State VAT.

The 56th GST Council meeting rationalised rates with effect from **22 September 2025**. The 12% and 28% slabs were removed for most goods.

| Slab (CGST + SGST or IGST) | Typical items |
| --- | --- |
| Nil | Fresh food, unbranded staples, specified essentials, individual life and health insurance |
| 0.25% / 3% | Rough diamonds; gold, silver and jewellery |
| 5% (merit rate) | Most items of mass consumption, many items earlier at 12%; restaurant service (without ITC) |
| 18% (standard rate) | Most goods and services, including many items earlier at 28% such as small cars and air conditioners |
| 40% (special rate) | Luxury and sin goods such as aerated sugared drinks, large cars and specified tobacco products |

Compensation cess was phased out after the rationalisation; it continued only on specified tobacco products for a transition period. Always take the rate from the question or from the current notification, because item-level rates change often.

lesson.heading: Reverse charge: sections 9(3), 9(4), 9(5) and 5(3) to 5(5) IGST
lesson.body:
Under **reverse charge** the recipient pays the tax. It must be paid in cash (electronic cash ledger), and the recipient may take ITC of it if otherwise eligible. Threshold exemption does not apply: a person liable under reverse charge must register (section 24).

Main services under section 9(3) (Notification 13/2017-CT(R), as amended):

| Service | Supplier | Recipient who pays |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goods transport agency (GTA), where GTA has not opted to pay forward charge | GTA | Factory, society, co-operative, registered person, body corporate, partnership firm, casual taxable person |
| Legal services | Individual advocate or firm of advocates | Any business entity (except small entities with turnover within the exemption limit, where the service is exempt) |
| Sponsorship services | Any person | Body corporate or partnership firm |
| Services by a director | Director | The company or body corporate |
| Services by insurance agent | Insurance agent | Insurance company |
| Security services | Person other than a body corporate | Registered person (with stated exceptions) |
| Renting of residential dwelling | Any person | Registered person |
| Renting of immovable property other than residential dwelling | Unregistered person | Registered person (other than a composition taxpayer) |

Goods under reverse charge include cashew nuts (not shelled or peeled), raw cotton, tobacco leaves and used vehicles or seized goods sold by the Government.

Section 9(4) lets the Government notify specified classes of registered persons who pay tax on supplies received from unregistered persons (used for promoters of real estate projects). Section 9(5) makes the **electronic commerce operator** liable for notified services supplied through it: passenger transport, accommodation, housekeeping and restaurant services.

**Common mistakes:** paying reverse charge tax through the credit ledger; forgetting that an advocate's fee is under reverse charge only when the recipient is a business entity; treating a gift above ₹50,000 to an employee as outside GST; and taxing a mixed supply at the principal item's rate instead of the highest rate.

keyPoints: Section 7: supply for consideration in course or furtherance of business; Schedule I covers 4 cases without consideration (assets with ITC, related or distinct persons, principal-agent, import of services from related person).
Employer's gifts to an employee up to ₹50,000 per financial year are not supply.
Composite supply (2(30)): rate of principal supply. Mixed supply (2(74)): highest rate among the items.
Schedule III: employee services, sale of land, merchant trade, sale of warehoused goods and high seas sale before home clearance, actionable claims other than the 6 specified ones.
Section 9(1) CGST cap 20%, section 5(1) IGST cap 40%. Rates from 22 September 2025: 5% merit, 18% standard, 40% special, plus Nil, 0.25% and 3%.
Reverse charge tax is paid only in cash; ITC is available to the recipient. Section 9(5) puts tax on the e-commerce operator for notified services.

cases.title: Case: Kavya Events Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
Kavya Events Pvt Ltd is registered in Pune, Maharashtra, and also holds a separate registration for its branch in Bengaluru, Karnataka. Its aggregate turnover last year was ₹14 crore. In October it had these transactions (values exclude GST):

| No. | Transaction | Value (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Diwali gifts of a laptop to each of 5 senior employees (₹60,000 per laptop); ITC was availed on the laptops | 3,00,000 |
| 2 | Sound equipment sent free of cost to the Bengaluru branch for its own events; open market value | 4,00,000 |
| 3 | Fees paid to an individual advocate in Pune for contract drafting | 1,20,000 |
| 4 | Corporate event package (venue, decor, catering, sound) for a client at one lump sum price | 8,00,000 |

Assume legal services are taxable at 18% and the equipment at 18%.

questions.prompt: A shop sells a festive pack containing chocolates, a fruit juice and a toy, for one price. The items are not naturally bundled. How is the pack taxed?
options: At the rate applicable to the item with the highest value
At the highest rate applicable to any item in the pack
At the rate of the principal supply
Each item at its own rate, by apportioning the price
questions.explanation: Items supplied together for a single price that are not naturally bundled form a mixed supply (section 2(74)). Section 8(b) taxes a mixed supply at the rate of the item that attracts the highest rate. The principal supply test applies only to composite supply.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum rate at which IGST can be levied under section 5(1) of the IGST Act?
questions.explanation: Section 5(1) IGST caps the rate at 40%. Section 9(1) CGST caps CGST at 20%, so CGST plus SGST also reaches a maximum of 40%. The 40% special rate is now in use for luxury and sin goods after the September 2025 rationalisation.

questions.prompt: How should transaction 1 (laptops gifted to employees) be treated?
options: Not a supply, as gifts to employees are covered by Schedule III
Not a supply, as there is no consideration
A supply under Schedule I, as the gift to each employee exceeds ₹50,000 in the year
A supply only if the employees are related persons under the Companies Act
questions.explanation: Employer and employee are related persons (explanation to section 15). Schedule I para 2 treats supply between related persons without consideration as supply, but its proviso excludes gifts up to ₹50,000 per employee per financial year. Each laptop is ₹60,000, so each gift is a supply. Schedule III para 1 covers services by employee to employer, not gifts by employer.

questions.prompt: Which tax applies to transaction 2 (equipment sent to the Bengaluru branch free of cost)?
options: No tax, because a branch transfer without consideration is not a supply
CGST and SGST of Maharashtra, because the supplier is in Pune
IGST, because it is a supply between distinct persons in different States
IGST under reverse charge payable by the Bengaluru branch
questions.explanation: Establishments of the same person with separate registrations are distinct persons (section 25(4)). Schedule I para 2 makes supply between distinct persons a supply even without consideration. The goods move from Maharashtra to Karnataka, so it is an inter-State supply liable to IGST under forward charge.

questions.prompt: A high seas sale of imported goods, by endorsement of the bill of lading before the goods are cleared for home consumption, is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services.
questions.explanation: Schedule III para 8(b) covers supply of goods by the consignee to any other person by endorsement of documents of title after dispatch from the port of origin outside India but before clearance for home consumption. IGST is paid once, at the time of customs clearance.

questions.prompt: Pick every service on which the registered recipient, a private limited company with turnover of ₹50 crore, pays GST under reverse charge.
options: Sitting fees paid to an independent director
Fees paid to a firm of advocates for a court case
Sponsorship of a sports event organised by a trust
Fees paid to a chartered accountant firm for statutory audit
Freight paid to a GTA that has not opted to pay tax under forward charge
questions.explanation: Director services to a company, legal services by an advocate or firm of advocates to a business entity, sponsorship services to a body corporate and GTA services (where the GTA has not opted for forward charge) are under reverse charge. Chartered accountancy services are under forward charge.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: composite supply is defined in section ___ of the CGST Act.
questions.explanation: Section 2(30) defines composite supply and section 2(90) defines principal supply. Mixed supply is in section 2(74). Section 8 gives the tax treatment for both.

questions.prompt: Compute the total GST payable on the gift box (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: A dealer in Chennai sells, within Tamil Nadu, a gift box for a single price of ₹25,000 (excluding GST). It contains sweets (rate 5%), a decorative steel bowl (rate 18%) and aerated sugared beverages (rate 40%). The items are not naturally bundled.
questions.explanation:
Mixed supply at a single price: the whole value is taxed at the highest rate.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Value of mixed supply | 25,000 |
| GST at 40% (CGST 20% + SGST 20%) | 10,000 |

CGST ₹5,000 and SGST ₹5,000; total ₹10,000.

questions.data:
Akash Steel Ltd, a registered company with turnover of ₹80 crore, received these services in a month (values exclude GST):

| Service | Value (₹) | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legal fees to an individual advocate | 2,50,000 | 18% |
| Freight to a GTA that has not opted for forward charge | 60,000 | 5% |
| Sponsorship of a cricket tournament | 1,00,000 | 18% |
| Sitting fees to a non-executive director | 40,000 | 18% |
| Audit fees to a CA firm | 3,00,000 | 18% |
questions.explanation:
| Service | Reverse charge? | Tax (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legal fees 2,50,000 x 18% | Yes | 45,000 |
| GTA 60,000 x 5% | Yes | 3,000 |
| Sponsorship 1,00,000 x 18% | Yes | 18,000 |
| Director fees 40,000 x 18% | Yes | 7,200 |
| Audit fees | No, forward charge | - |
| **Total reverse charge tax** | | **73,200** |

questions.prompt: Compute the GST Kavya Events must pay under reverse charge on transaction 3 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.explanation:
Legal services by an individual advocate to a business entity whose turnover exceeds the exemption limit are taxable under reverse charge.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Legal fees | 1,20,000 |
| CGST 9% | 10,800 |
| SGST 9% | 10,800 |
| **Total** | **21,600** |

Both parties are in Maharashtra, so CGST and SGST apply.

questions.prompt: How is transaction 4 (corporate event package at a lump sum price) taxed?
options: As a mixed supply at the highest rate among venue, decor, catering and sound
As a composite supply at the rate applicable to event management, the principal supply
Each element at its own rate, as the elements are separately identifiable
Catering is exempt and the balance is taxed at the event management rate
questions.explanation: Venue, decor, catering and sound are naturally bundled in an event management package, and a client buys them as one service. The package is a composite supply with event management as the principal supply (section 8(a)).

questions.prompt: Compute the CGST, SGST and IGST payable by M/s Rao Traders for the month, showing forward and reverse charge separately.
questions.data:
M/s Rao Traders, Hyderabad (Telangana), is a regular registered taxpayer. Transactions in the month (values exclude GST):

| No. | Transaction | Value (₹) | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Sale of goods within Telangana | 12,00,000 | 18% |
| 2 | Sale of goods to a dealer in Pune | 4,00,000 | 5% |
| 3 | Export of goods under LUT | 6,00,000 | 18% |
| 4 | Legal fees to an advocate in Hyderabad | 1,00,000 | 18% |
| 5 | Freight to a Telangana GTA not opting for forward charge | 40,000 | 5% |
| 6 | Goods sent free to its own Bengaluru branch (separately registered); value under rule 28 | 2,00,000 | 18% |

Ignore ITC.
questions.answer:
**Forward charge**

| No. | Treatment | CGST (₹) | SGST (₹) | IGST (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Intra-State supply | 1,08,000 | 1,08,000 | - |
| 2 | Inter-State supply | - | - | 20,000 |
| 3 | Zero-rated export under LUT (section 16 IGST) | - | - | Nil |
| 6 | Supply to distinct person, Schedule I para 2; inter-State | - | - | 36,000 |
| | **Sub-total** | **1,08,000** | **1,08,000** | **56,000** |

**Reverse charge (to be paid in cash)**

| No. | Treatment | CGST (₹) | SGST (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | Legal services to business entity | 9,000 | 9,000 |
| 5 | GTA under reverse charge at 5% | 1,000 | 1,000 |
| | **Sub-total** | **10,000** | **10,000** |

**Total liability:** CGST ₹1,18,000, SGST ₹1,18,000 and IGST ₹56,000, total ₹2,92,000. The forward charge liability can be set off against ITC; the reverse charge liability of ₹20,000 must be paid through the electronic cash ledger. The reverse charge tax is then available as ITC in the same month.

questions.prompt: State whether each of these is a composite supply, a mixed supply or neither, and the rate principle that applies.
questions.data:
(a) A hotel room at ₹6,000 per night including breakfast.
(b) A laptop sold with a carry bag at one price.
(c) A coaching institute's course fee that includes printed study material.
(d) A shop selling a combo of a water bottle, a lunch box and a pencil pouch at one price.
(e) A courier company collecting freight plus a separate charge for packing the goods it carries.
questions.answer:
| Case | Nature | Rate principle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a) | Composite; accommodation is principal, breakfast is ancillary | Rate of accommodation service |
| (b) | Composite; laptop is principal, bag is ancillary | Rate of the laptop |
| (c) | Composite; coaching is principal, material is ancillary | Rate of coaching service |
| (d) | Mixed; items are independent and could be sold separately | Highest rate among the three items |
| (e) | Composite; transport is principal, packing is ancillary | Rate of courier service |

The test is whether the items are naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business. A single price is necessary for mixed supply but does not create a composite supply by itself.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between composite supply and mixed supply under GST with examples, and explain how tax liability is determined for each.
questions.answer:
- **Definitions:** composite supply (section 2(30)) is two or more taxable supplies that are naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business, one of which is the principal supply (section 2(90)). Mixed supply (section 2(74)) is two or more individual supplies made together for a single price where the combination is not a composite supply.
- **Test:** natural bundling, judged by consumer perception, trade practice, advertising as a package and whether one item is ancillary.
- **Tax (section 8):** a composite supply is treated as a supply of the principal supply; a mixed supply is treated as a supply of the item that attracts the highest rate.
- **Examples:** goods with packing, transport and insurance (composite, rate of the goods); a gift hamper of sweets, dry fruits and an aerated drink at one price (mixed, rate of the drink).
- Works contract and restaurant food are treated as services by Schedule II, so the section 8 test is not needed for them.

questions.prompt: What activities does Schedule III to the CGST Act treat as neither supply of goods nor supply of services? Explain the treatment of actionable claims.
questions.answer:
- Services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment; services of courts and tribunals; functions of MPs, MLAs and local body members and of constitutional office holders; funeral, burial, crematorium and mortuary services.
- Sale of land and sale of a building after the completion certificate (subject to para 5(b) of Schedule II).
- Actionable claims, **other than specified actionable claims** (betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery and online money gaming), which remain taxable as goods.
- Merchant trade: supply of goods from one place outside India to another without the goods entering India.
- Sale of warehoused goods before home clearance, and high seas sale by endorsement of documents of title before home clearance.
- Effect: no GST is payable on these activities. For ITC reversal under section 17(3), the value of exempt supply excludes Schedule III activities except those specifically brought in, the main one being sale of land and building (para 5).

chapters.title: Place of Supply under the IGST Act
chapters.summary: Inter-State versus intra-State supply, place of supply of goods (sections 10 and 11), of domestic services (section 12) and of cross-border services (section 13), including the omission of the intermediary rule by the Finance Act 2026.
chapters.lawAsOf: IGST Act as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Why place of supply matters: sections 7 and 8 IGST
lesson.body:
Place of supply (POS) decides **which tax** applies and **which State** gets it. Compare the location of the supplier with the POS:

| Location of supplier vs POS | Nature | Tax |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same State or same Union territory | Intra-State (section 8) | CGST + SGST/UTGST |
| Different States or UTs | Inter-State (section 7) | IGST |
| Supplier in India, POS outside India | Inter-State (section 7(5)(a)) | IGST, or zero-rated if it is an export |
| Supply to or by an SEZ developer or unit | Inter-State (section 7(5)(b)), even within one State | IGST, zero-rated under section 16 |
| Import of goods or services | Inter-State (section 7(2), 7(4)) | IGST |

Supplies to a foreign tourist who carries goods out of India are inter-State (section 7(5)(c)).

If tax is paid as CGST + SGST on a supply later held to be inter-State, the taxpayer pays IGST and claims a refund of the wrongly paid tax under section 77 CGST / section 19 IGST; no interest is charged on the IGST.

lesson.heading: Goods: sections 10 and 11
lesson.body:
| Situation | Place of supply |
| --- | --- |
| Supply involves movement of goods (section 10(1)(a)) | Location where movement terminates for delivery to the recipient |
| Goods delivered to a person on the direction of a third person, before or during movement (bill to ship to, 10(1)(b)) | **Principal place of business of the third person** who directs |
| No movement of goods (10(1)(c)) | Location of the goods at the time of delivery |
| Goods assembled or installed at site (10(1)(d)) | Place of assembly or installation |
| Goods supplied on board a conveyance (vessel, aircraft, train, motor vehicle) (10(1)(e)) | Location where the goods are **taken on board** |
| Supply to an unregistered person (10(1)(ca)) | Address of the recipient recorded in the invoice; if none, location of the supplier |
| Import of goods (section 11(a)) | Location of the importer |
| Export of goods (section 11(b)) | Location outside India |

**Worked example.** A Lucknow dealer (U.P.) sells goods to a Patna buyer (Bihar), who asks that the goods be delivered to his customer in Kanpur (U.P.). Under section 10(1)(b) the POS is Bihar, the principal place of business of the Patna buyer. The Lucknow dealer charges IGST, even though the goods never leave U.P.

lesson.heading: Domestic services: section 12 (supplier and recipient both in India)
lesson.body:
**General rule (section 12(2)):** registered recipient: location of the recipient. Unregistered recipient: location of the recipient where his address is on record, otherwise location of the supplier.

| Service | Place of supply |
| --- | --- |
| Immovable property: construction, architects, interior decorators, lodging, renting, events in a property (12(3)) | Location of the immovable property or boat; if the property is outside India, location of the recipient |
| Restaurant, catering, personal grooming, beauty, fitness, health services (12(4)) | Location where the services are actually performed |
| Training and performance appraisal (12(5)) | Registered recipient: his location. Otherwise: where performed |
| Admission to events, amusement parks (12(6)) | Place where the event is held or the park is located |
| Organising events (12(7)) | Registered recipient: his location. Otherwise: where the event is held; if held outside India, location of the recipient |
| Transport of goods, including mail and courier (12(8)) | Registered recipient: his location. Otherwise: where goods are handed over for transport |
| Passenger transport (12(9)) | Registered recipient: his location. Otherwise: where the passenger embarks for a continuous journey |
| Telecom (12(11)) | Fixed line: where installed. Post-paid mobile: billing address on record. Pre-paid: where the recharge is sold |
| Banking and financial services to account holders (12(12)) | Location of the recipient on the supplier's records, otherwise supplier's location |
| Insurance (12(13)) | Registered: his location. Otherwise: recipient's location on record |

lesson.heading: Cross-border services: section 13 and the Finance Act 2026 change
lesson.body:
Section 13 applies when **either** the supplier or the recipient is outside India.

| Service | Place of supply |
| --- | --- |
| General rule (13(2)) | Location of the recipient; if not available in the ordinary course of business, location of the supplier |
| Services on goods made physically available by the recipient, or services needing the physical presence of the individual (13(3)) | Where actually performed. Goods temporarily imported for repairs and re-exported are excluded |
| Services directly related to immovable property (13(4)) | Location of the property |
| Admission to or organisation of events (13(5)) | Place where the event is held |
| Banking company, financial institution or NBFC services to account holders (13(8)(a)) | Location of the supplier |
| Hiring of means of transport up to one month (13(8)(c)) | Location of the supplier |
| Transport of goods, other than mail or courier (13(9)) | Destination of the goods |
| Passenger transport (13(10)) | Place where the passenger embarks |
| Online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) (13(12)) | Location of the recipient |

**Intermediary services.** Section 13(8)(b) placed intermediary services at the location of the supplier, so an Indian agent arranging supplies for a foreign principal could not export its service. The **Finance Act 2026 omitted clause (b) of section 13(8)**. Intermediary services now fall under the general rule in section 13(2): POS is the location of the recipient. An Indian intermediary serving a foreign client can treat the service as an **export** if the five conditions of section 2(6) are met. The definition of intermediary in section 2(13) is unchanged.

**Export of services (section 2(6)):** supplier located in India; recipient located outside India; POS outside India; payment received in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees where RBI permits; supplier and recipient are not merely establishments of the same person (explanation 1 to section 8).

**Common mistakes:** applying section 12 when the recipient is abroad; using the bill-to address instead of the third person's principal place of business in a bill to ship to supply; and treating supply to an SEZ unit in the same State as intra-State.

keyPoints: Supplier location vs POS: same State is intra-State (CGST + SGST); different States, imports, exports and SEZ supplies are inter-State (IGST).
Goods: movement ends (10(1)(a)); bill to ship to: third person's principal place of business (10(1)(b)); on board conveyance: where taken on board (10(1)(e)).
Section 12: immovable property, restaurant, admission and grooming follow the place; training, events, goods transport and passenger transport follow the registered recipient.
Section 13 default is location of the recipient; exceptions for physical performance, immovable property, events, banking to account holders and short-term hire of transport.
Finance Act 2026 omitted section 13(8)(b): intermediary services now follow the recipient's location, so they can qualify as export.
Export of services needs all 5 conditions of section 2(6) IGST, including convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits).

Madhya Pradesh, the location of the supplier

questions.explanation: Section 10(1)(b) IGST: where goods are delivered to a recipient or any other person on the direction of a third person, the third person is deemed to receive the goods and POS is that person's principal place of business. Meera is in Rajasthan, so Rajan charges IGST.

questions.prompt: A caterer from Delhi provides catering at a wedding in Agra (U.P.) for a Delhi resident who is not registered. What is the place of supply?
options: Delhi, location of the recipient
Delhi, location of the supplier
Uttar Pradesh, where the service is performed
Uttar Pradesh only if the bill exceeds ₹50,000
questions.explanation: Section 12(4) IGST: restaurant, food and catering services are supplied at the location where they are actually performed. Agra is in U.P., so the Delhi caterer charges IGST.

questions.prompt: What is the GST treatment of supply 1 (commission from the US buyer) after the Finance Act 2026?
options: Intra-State supply in Maharashtra, as POS of intermediary services is the location of the supplier
Export of services, as POS is now the location of the recipient and the other section 2(6) conditions are met
Not a supply, as the goods are supplied by the textile exporter
Import of services, taxable under reverse charge
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 omitted section 13(8)(b) IGST, so intermediary services fall under section 13(2): POS is the location of the recipient, the US. The supplier is in India, the recipient is outside India, payment is in foreign exchange and they are not establishments of one person, so it is a zero-rated export of services.

questions.prompt: Which tax applies to supply 2 (dealer conference in Dubai for the Delhi company)?
options: No tax, as the event is held outside India
IGST, as POS is Delhi, the location of the registered recipient
CGST and SGST of Maharashtra
IGST, as POS is outside India
questions.explanation: Both supplier and recipient are in India, so section 12 applies, not section 13. Under section 12(7)(a)(i), when an event is organised for a registered person, POS is the location of that person: Delhi. The supplier is in Maharashtra, so IGST applies.

questions.prompt: Supply of goods by a Chennai manufacturer to an SEZ unit located in Chennai is an intra-State supply liable to CGST and SGST.
questions.explanation: Section 7(5)(b) IGST treats any supply of goods or services to or by an SEZ developer or SEZ unit as inter-State, even within one State. It is a zero-rated supply under section 16 IGST, made under LUT or with payment of IGST and refund.

questions.prompt: Which of these are conditions for a supply to be an export of services under section 2(6) of the IGST Act?
options: The supplier is located in India
The recipient is located outside India
The place of supply is outside India
Payment is received in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees where permitted by RBI
The supplier has obtained an export promotion authorisation from DGFT
questions.explanation: Section 2(6) has five conditions: the four listed plus that the supplier and recipient are not merely establishments of a distinct person. No DGFT authorisation is needed.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the Finance Act 2026 omitted clause (b) of section 13(___) of the IGST Act, which dealt with intermediary services.
questions.explanation: Section 13(8) had three clauses: (a) banking and NBFC services to account holders, (b) intermediary services and (c) hiring of means of transport up to one month, all at the location of the supplier. Clause (b) is omitted; (a) and (c) remain.

questions.prompt: Compute the IGST payable by the interior decorator (round to the nearest rupee). Enter 0 if no IGST is payable.
questions.data: An interior decorator registered in Hyderabad (Telangana) designs the interiors of a holiday villa in Goa for a company registered in Mumbai (Maharashtra). Fee: ₹5,00,000 excluding GST. Rate: 18%.
questions.explanation:
Section 12(3)(a): services of interior decorators directly in relation to immovable property are supplied at the location of the property, Goa, whatever the recipient's registration.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier: Telangana; POS: Goa | Inter-State |
| IGST 18% of 5,00,000 | 90,000 |

Utsav Events is registered in Delhi. Fees exclude GST; rate 18% for all.

| Supply | Fee (₹) |

| Organised a wedding in Jaipur for an unregistered Delhi resident | 2,00,000 |
| Training session held in Delhi for an unregistered individual from Chandigarh | 1,00,000 |

| Launch for registered person (12(7)(a)(i)) | Delhi | Intra | 1,80,000 | - |
| Wedding for unregistered person (12(7)(a)(ii)) | Rajasthan, where held | Inter | - | 36,000 |
| Training for unregistered person (12(5)(b)) | Delhi, where performed | Intra | 18,000 | - |

questions.explanation:
Recipient is outside India, so section 13 applies. Training delivered in person needs the physical presence of the individuals, so under section 13(3)(b) POS is where the service is actually performed: Mumbai. POS is in India, so it is not an export. Supplier and POS are both in Maharashtra.

options: Singapore, location of the recipient
Maharashtra, location of the immovable property
Maharashtra, location of the supplier
Outside India, as consideration is from abroad
questions.explanation: Section 13(4): services directly in relation to immovable property, including services of experts, architects and approvals, are supplied at the location of the property. The factory is in Pune, so POS is Maharashtra and the supply is not an export.

questions.prompt: A Kochi company hires out a yacht for 10 days to a tourist from France who is not in business. What is the place of supply?
options: France, location of the recipient
Location of the supplier, Kerala
The place where the yacht is used
Location of the bank receiving the payment
questions.explanation: Section 13(8)(c): hiring of means of transport, including yachts, up to a period of one month is supplied at the location of the supplier. This clause was not affected by the Finance Act 2026.

questions.prompt: Determine the place of supply and state whether CGST + SGST or IGST applies to each supply by Bose Enterprises, registered in Kolkata (West Bengal). Give the section.
questions.data:
(a) Sale of goods to a Patna (Bihar) dealer, delivered on his instructions to his customer in Howrah (West Bengal).
(b) Packaged food sold on a train running from Kolkata to Delhi; the food was taken on board at Kolkata.
(c) Architectural design of a resort in Bhutan for a company registered in Kolkata.
(d) Road transport of goods from Kolkata to Ranchi (Jharkhand) for an unregistered person.
(e) Post-paid mobile service for an individual whose billing address is in Guwahati (Assam).
(f) Air ticket from Kolkata to Chennai for an unregistered individual.
questions.answer:
| Supply | Section | POS | Tax |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (a) Bill to ship to | 10(1)(b) | Bihar, principal place of business of the Patna dealer | IGST |
| (b) Goods on board a conveyance | 10(1)(e) | West Bengal, where taken on board | CGST + SGST |
| (c) Immovable property outside India | 12(3), proviso | West Bengal, location of the recipient | CGST + SGST |
| (d) Goods transport for unregistered person | 12(8)(b) | West Bengal, where goods are handed over | CGST + SGST |
| (e) Post-paid telecom | 12(11)(c)(ii) | Assam, billing address on record | IGST |
| (f) Passenger transport for unregistered person | 12(9) | West Bengal, where the passenger embarks | CGST + SGST |

Section 12 applies to all the services because both supplier and recipient are in India.

questions.prompt: Explain the change made by the Finance Act 2026 to the place of supply of intermediary services and its effect on Indian intermediaries serving foreign clients.
questions.answer:
- **Earlier position:** section 13(8)(b) IGST deemed the POS of intermediary services (section 2(13): a broker or agent who arranges or facilitates supplies between two or more persons, excluding a person who supplies on his own account) to be the location of the supplier. An Indian intermediary serving a foreign principal therefore had POS in India and could not export the service; IGST or CGST + SGST was payable and litigation was frequent.
- **Amendment:** the Finance Act 2026 omitted section 13(8)(b). Intermediary services now follow the general rule in section 13(2): location of the recipient.
- **Effect:** where the recipient is abroad and all conditions of section 2(6) are met (supplier in India, recipient outside India, POS outside India, payment in convertible foreign exchange or permitted INR, not establishments of the same person), the supply is an export and zero-rated under section 16. The supplier can export under LUT and claim refund of unutilised ITC.
- The definition of intermediary is unchanged, so the principal-versus-agent test still decides whether section 13(2) or another rule applies. For domestic intermediaries (both parties in India), section 12 continues to apply.

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions for determining the place of supply of goods other than imports and exports under section 10 of the IGST Act.
questions.answer:
- **10(1)(a):** where the supply involves movement of goods, by the supplier, recipient or any other person, POS is the location where movement terminates for delivery to the recipient.
- **10(1)(b):** where goods are delivered to the recipient or any other person on the direction of a third person (by transfer of documents of title or otherwise), the third person is deemed to have received the goods and POS is his principal place of business.
- **10(1)(c):** where there is no movement of goods, POS is the location of the goods at the time of delivery.
- **10(1)(ca):** supply to an unregistered person: the address recorded in the invoice; if none, the location of the supplier.
- **10(1)(d):** goods assembled or installed at site: place of assembly or installation.
- **10(1)(e):** goods supplied on board a conveyance: location where the goods are taken on board.
- **10(2):** where POS cannot be determined under these rules, it is decided in the manner prescribed on the Council's recommendation.

chapters.title: Exemptions and Valuation in Depth
chapters.summary: Exemption power under section 11 and the main service exemptions, transaction value under section 15 including the post-supply discount amendment of 1 November 2026, and the CGST valuation rules 27 to 35.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act and Rules as amended by Finance Act 2026 (sections 15 and 34 amendments in force from 1 November 2026)

lesson.heading: Exemptions: section 11 and key notified exemptions
lesson.body:
Section 11(1) lets the Government, on the Council's recommendation, exempt goods or services **absolutely** or **subject to conditions**. Where an exemption is absolute, a registered person **cannot** pay tax on that supply. Section 11(2) allows special orders for exceptional cases. Exemptions for services are mainly in Notification 12/2017-CT(R), as amended.

Examples of exempt services that are regularly examined:

| Service | Condition or note |
| --- | --- |
| Health care by a clinical establishment, an authorised medical practitioner or para-medics | Room rent above a notified limit (non-ICU) is excluded |
| Education by an educational institution to its students | Pre-school to higher secondary, education recognised by law, approved vocational courses |
| Renting of residential dwelling for use as residence | Exempt unless rented to a registered person (then reverse charge) |
| Legal services by an advocate or firm of advocates | To an individual not in business, or to a business entity with turnover within the registration threshold |
| Individual life insurance and individual health insurance, including reinsurance of these | Exempt from 22 September 2025 |
| Services by the Government or a local authority | Most services to individuals; services to business entities are taxable under reverse charge, with stated exceptions |
| Charitable activities by entities registered under the Income-tax Act | Activities as defined in the notification |
| Transport of goods by road | Exempt except by a GTA or courier agency |
| Agriculture support services | Cultivation, harvesting, warehousing of agricultural produce, and similar |

A nil-rated or exempt supply is still a supply: it counts in aggregate turnover and requires ITC reversal under section 17(2).

lesson.heading: Transaction value: section 15
lesson.body:
Value is the **transaction value** (price actually paid or payable) where the supplier and recipient are **not related** and **price is the sole consideration** (section 15(1)).

**Included in value (section 15(2)):**

- Taxes, duties, cesses and fees under any other law, other than GST and compensation cess, if charged separately.
- Any amount the supplier is liable to pay but which the recipient has paid, and which is not included in the price.
- Incidental expenses, including commission and packing, charged by the supplier, and any amount charged for anything done by the supplier at or before delivery.
- Interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment of consideration.
- Subsidies directly linked to the price, **except** subsidies provided by the Central and State Governments.

**Discounts (section 15(3)):**

- (a) Discount given before or at the time of supply and recorded in the invoice: excluded.
- (b) Discount given after supply: as substituted by the Finance Act 2026 (in force from **1 November 2026**), excluded if a **credit note is issued under section 34** and the recipient **reverses the ITC** attributable to the discount. The earlier requirements of a prior agreement and linkage to specific invoices are removed. Section 34(1) now expressly allows a credit note for such a discount.

**Worked example.**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| List price | 1,00,000 |
| Less: trade discount shown in invoice | (10,000) |
| Add: packing charged separately | 2,000 |
| Add: inspection fee payable by supplier but paid by buyer to the inspector | 3,000 |
| Add: freight to buyer's site (contract is for delivered price) | 4,000 |
| Government subsidy received by supplier | Not added |
| **Value of supply** | **99,000** |

lesson.heading: Valuation rules 27 to 35
lesson.body:
Where section 15(1) does not apply (related parties, non-monetary consideration, or notified supplies), section 15(4) and (5) send you to the rules.

| Rule | Situation | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 27 | Consideration not wholly in money | Open market value (OMV); else money plus money value of non-monetary consideration; else value of like kind and quality; else rule 30 or 31 |
| 28(1) | Related or distinct persons (not agents) | OMV; else like kind and quality; else rule 30 or 31. At the supplier's option, **90% of the price charged by the recipient to unrelated customers** where the recipient resells the goods as such. Where the recipient can take **full ITC**, the invoice value is deemed OMV |
| 28(2) | Corporate guarantee to a related person | 1% of the amount guaranteed per year, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher |
| 29 | Supply through an agent | OMV, or at the supplier's option 90% of the price charged by the recipient to unrelated customers |
| 30 | Cost-based | **110% of cost** of production, manufacture or acquisition, or cost of provision of service |
| 31 | Residual | Reasonable means consistent with section 15 and the rules; for services the supplier may skip rule 30 |
| 32(2) | Purchase or sale of foreign currency by a money changer | (Buying or selling rate minus RBI reference rate) x units of currency |
| 32(3) | Air travel agent | **5% of basic fare** (domestic) and **10% of basic fare** (international) |
| 32(5) | Second-hand goods (no significant processing, no ITC taken) | Selling price minus purchase price; ignore a negative value |
| 33 | Expenses of a **pure agent** | Excluded if the conditions are met |
| 35 | Value inclusive of tax | Tax = value x rate / (100 + rate) |

**Pure agent (rule 33):** the supplier acts as pure agent of the recipient when he pays a third party on the recipient's authorisation; the payment is shown separately in the invoice; the supplies procured are in addition to his own services; he does not hold title or use the supply for his own interest; and he recovers only the actual amount paid. Example: a visa fee paid by a travel agent to an embassy and recovered at actuals.

lesson.heading: Exam approach and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Lay out a valuation answer as a working table: start with the contract price, list each item with **Included / Excluded** and the section or rule, and then compute tax. Examiners give marks for the reason, not only the figure.

Common mistakes:

- Deducting a post-supply discount without checking the credit note and ITC reversal conditions, or applying the pre-November 2026 conditions to a discount given after 1 November 2026.
- Adding a Government subsidy to value. Only non-Government subsidies linked to price are included.
- Using rule 28's 90% option where the recipient does not resell the goods as such.
- Taxing the full air fare in an air travel agent's hands instead of 5% or 10% of the basic fare.
- Forgetting rule 35 when the amount given is inclusive of GST: back out tax using rate / (100 + rate).

keyPoints: Section 11: absolute exemptions cannot be waived by paying tax; exempt supplies still count in aggregate turnover.
Section 15(2) adds taxes other than GST, supplier's liabilities paid by recipient, incidental expenses, late payment interest and non-Government price-linked subsidies.
Post-supply discount (section 15(3)(b), from 1 November 2026): credit note under section 34 plus recipient's ITC reversal; prior agreement and invoice linkage no longer needed.
Rule 28: OMV, or 90% of recipient's resale price; invoice value is OMV where recipient gets full ITC. Rule 28(2) corporate guarantee: 1% per year or actual, higher.
Rule 30: 110% of cost. Rule 32(3): air travel agent 5% domestic / 10% international basic fare. Rule 32(5): margin on second-hand goods.
Rule 33 pure agent: separate invoice line, authorisation, actual recovery, no title or own use.

cases.title: Case: TravelWise Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
TravelWise Pvt Ltd, registered in Bengaluru, is an air travel agent and an authorised money changer. Data for January 2027 (all GST at 18%):

| Item | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Basic fare of domestic air tickets booked | 40,00,000 |
| Basic fare of international air tickets booked | 30,00,000 |
| Airport and fuel charges included in the tickets | 6,00,000 |
| Visa fees paid to consulates on clients' authorisation, shown separately and recovered at actuals | 2,50,000 |

On one day it sold USD 1,000 to a customer at ₹86.50 per USD when the RBI reference rate was ₹86.00. TravelWise has not opted for the alternative fixed-value method for money changing.

questions.prompt: In December 2026 a supplier allows a buyer a turnover discount on sales of the previous quarter, without any prior agreement. When can the discount be excluded from the value of supply under section 15(3)(b) as amended?
options: Never, because there was no agreement at or before the time of supply
Only if the discount can be linked to specific invoices
If a credit note is issued under section 34 and the recipient reverses the attributable ITC
Only if the discount is shown on the original tax invoice
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 substituted section 15(3)(b), effective 1 November 2026. A post-supply discount is excluded if a credit note is issued under section 34 and the recipient reverses the ITC attributable to it. Prior agreement and invoice linkage are no longer required.

questions.prompt: Which of these services is exempt from GST after the September 2025 changes?
options: Group health insurance for employees of a company
Individual health insurance policy bought by a salaried person
Motor vehicle insurance for a private car
Fire insurance of a residential flat
questions.explanation: With effect from 22 September 2025, individual life insurance and individual health insurance policies (and their reinsurance) were exempted. Group policies and general insurance such as motor and fire remain taxable.

questions.prompt: What is the value of TravelWise's supply on the sale of USD 1,000?
questions.explanation: Rule 32(2)(a): for purchase or sale of foreign currency where the RBI reference rate is available, value = (selling rate - RBI reference rate) x units. (86.50 - 86.00) x 1,000 = ₹500.

questions.prompt: How are the visa fees of ₹2,50,000 treated in TravelWise's value of supply?
options: Included, as all amounts recovered from clients are consideration
Excluded, as TravelWise acts as a pure agent under rule 33
Included at 5% of the amount, as for domestic tickets
Excluded only if the consulate is registered under GST
questions.explanation: The fees are paid to a third party on the client's authorisation, shown separately in the invoice and recovered at actuals, and the visa is the client's own supply. These are the rule 33 pure agent conditions, so the amount is excluded from value.

questions.prompt: Interest charged by a supplier for late payment of the price is not part of the value of supply, because it is a financial charge and not consideration for goods.
questions.explanation: Section 15(2)(d) includes interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration in the value of supply. It takes the rate of the main supply. (A separate exemption covers interest on loans, but not late payment interest on trade dues.)

questions.prompt: Which of these are included in the value of supply under section 15(2)?
options: Packing charges billed separately by the supplier
A subsidy from a private trade body that lowers the price charged
A subsidy received from the State Government linked to the price
Municipal tax payable by the supplier but paid by the buyer
CGST and SGST charged in the invoice
questions.explanation: Incidental expenses such as packing (15(2)(c)), non-Government price-linked subsidies (15(2)(e)) and the supplier's liabilities paid by the recipient (15(2)(b)) are included. Government subsidies are excluded by 15(2)(e), and GST itself is never part of the value.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under rule 30 of the CGST Rules, value is ___% of the cost of production, manufacture or acquisition of the goods.
questions.explanation: Rule 30 (cost-based method) values the supply at 110% of cost of production, manufacture, acquisition or provision of service. It applies when rules 27 to 29 cannot give the value.

The open market value cannot be determined. The branch makes some exempt supplies, so it cannot take full ITC. IGST rate: 18%.
questions.explanation:
Supply between distinct persons is valued under rule 28. As the branch resells as such, the supplier may opt for 90% of the price charged by the recipient to unrelated customers. The full ITC proviso does not apply.

questions.prompt: A registered dealer in used cars buys a car from an individual for ₹4,00,000 and sells it after cleaning for ₹3,70,000 without taking any ITC. What is the value of supply under rule 32(5)?
options: Nil
questions.explanation: Rule 32(5): for second-hand goods sold as such or after minor processing, where no ITC was availed, value is the selling price minus purchase price, and a negative value is ignored. 3,70,000 - 4,00,000 is negative, so the value is nil.

questions.prompt: The supplier received ₹1,18,000 inclusive of GST at 18%. Compute the GST included in this amount (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.explanation: Rule 35: tax = value inclusive of tax x rate / (100 + rate) = 1,18,000 x 18 / 118 = ₹18,000. The value of supply is ₹1,00,000.

questions.prompt: Compute the value of taxable supply and GST payable by Orion Packaging Ltd for the transactions below, giving reasons for inclusion or exclusion.
questions.data:
Orion Packaging Ltd, Pune, supplies cartons within Maharashtra at 18% GST. Details for one order:

| Item | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Price of cartons as per contract (before discount) | 8,00,000 |
| Discount of 2% shown in the invoice | |
| Design charges for printing artwork, billed separately | 25,000 |
| Freight for delivery to buyer (Orion's responsibility), billed separately | 15,000 |
| Late payment interest charged later | 6,000 |
| Post-supply volume discount given in December 2026 by credit note; buyer reversed the ITC | 20,000 |
| Subsidy from a State Government scheme | 30,000 |
questions.answer:
| Particulars | Treatment | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contract price | Transaction value | 8,00,000 |
| Less: 2% discount in invoice | Excluded, 15(3)(a) | (16,000) |
| Design charges | Included, done by supplier before delivery, 15(2)(c) | 25,000 |
| Freight | Included, incidental expense, 15(2)(c) | 15,000 |
| Late payment interest | Included, 15(2)(d) | 6,000 |
| Less: post-supply discount | Excluded, 15(3)(b) as amended; credit note issued and ITC reversed | (20,000) |
| State Government subsidy | Not included, 15(2)(e) | - |
| **Taxable value** | | **8,10,000** |
| CGST 9% | | 72,900 |
| SGST 9% | | 72,900 |
| **Total GST** | | **1,45,800** |

In practice the late payment interest and the credit note are reported in the period in which they arise, but the net value of this order is ₹8,10,000.

questions.prompt: Explain how a supply between related persons is valued under rule 28 of the CGST Rules, including the proviso for recipients eligible for full ITC.
questions.answer:
- Rule 28 applies where section 15(1) fails because the parties are related or distinct persons (other than supplies through an agent, which fall under rule 29).
- Value is (a) the open market value; (b) if not available, value of supply of goods or services of like kind and quality; (c) if neither, the value under rule 30 (110% of cost) or rule 31 (residual).
- **Option:** where the recipient supplies the goods as such, the supplier may value at 90% of the price charged by the recipient to its unrelated customers.
- **Proviso:** where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the value declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value. This makes stock transfers revenue-neutral and accepts the invoice value.
- **Rule 28(2):** a corporate guarantee to a related person (including a holding company guaranteeing a subsidiary's loan) is valued at 1% of the amount guaranteed per year, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher.
- Employer and employee are related persons; gifts up to ₹50,000 a year are not supply at all.

questions.prompt: Who is a pure agent under rule 33, and why does it matter for valuation?
questions.answer:
- A pure agent is a person who (a) enters into a contractual agreement with the recipient to act as his pure agent to incur expenditure in the course of supply; (b) neither intends to hold nor holds title to the goods or services procured; (c) does not use them for his own interest; and (d) receives only the actual amount incurred to procure them, in addition to his own fee.
- Expenditure incurred as pure agent is excluded from value only if: the supplier pays the third party on the recipient's authorisation; the payment is shown separately in the invoice; and the supplies procured from the third party are in addition to the services the supplier provides on his own account.
- Examples: registration fees paid by a CA on a client's behalf, visa fees paid by a travel agent, stamp duty paid by an advocate.
- If any condition fails, the expense becomes part of the supplier's value under section 15(2)(c) and carries GST at his rate.

chapters.summary: Conditions and time limits for ITC, blocked credits under section 17(5), apportionment under rules 42 and 43, Input Service Distributor, job work, sale of capital goods and the order of utilisation.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act and Rules as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Eligibility and conditions: section 16
lesson.body:
A registered person can take ITC on goods or services used or intended to be used **in the course or furtherance of business** (section 16(1)), only when **all** conditions of section 16(2) are met:

- (a) He holds a tax invoice or debit note.
- (aa) The details of the invoice are furnished by the supplier in GSTR-1 and communicated in **GSTR-2B** (rule 36(4) allows ITC only to that extent).
- (b) He has received the goods or services. Bill to ship to deliveries count as receipt. For goods received in lots, ITC is taken on receipt of the **last lot**.
- (ba) The ITC is not restricted in GSTR-2B under section 38.
- (c) The tax charged has been actually paid to the Government by the supplier.
- (d) He has furnished his return under section 39.

**Payment within 180 days:** if the recipient does not pay the supplier the value plus tax within 180 days of the invoice date, the ITC is reversed (added to output tax) with interest; it can be re-availed on payment. This does not apply to reverse charge supplies.

**Time limit (section 16(4)):** ITC on an invoice or debit note cannot be taken after **30 November following the end of the financial year** to which it relates, or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier.

**Depreciation:** if depreciation is claimed on the tax component of capital goods under the Income-tax law, ITC on that tax is not allowed (section 16(3)).

lesson.heading: Blocked credits: section 17(5)
lesson.body:
| Clause | Blocked | Exceptions (ITC allowed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a), (aa), (ab) | Motor vehicles for transport of persons with seating capacity of **13 or fewer** (including driver); vessels and aircraft; their insurance, repair and maintenance | Further supply of such vehicles; transport of passengers; imparting training on driving; vessels and aircraft for goods transport. Goods carriages are not blocked |
| (b)(i) | Food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, cosmetic and plastic surgery, leasing or hiring of motor vehicles, vessels and aircraft, life and health insurance | Same category of outward supply or part of a taxable composite or mixed supply; or where the employer is **obliged by law** to provide it |
| (b)(ii), (iii) | Membership of a club, health and fitness centre; travel benefits to employees on vacation (leave travel) | Where obligatory under law |
| (c) | Works contract services for construction of immovable property | Plant and machinery; input service for further supply of works contract |
| (d) | Goods or services received for construction of immovable property on own account, even if used in business | Plant and machinery |
| (e) | Tax paid under composition | - |
| (f) | Supplies received by a non-resident taxable person | Goods imported by him |
| (fa) | CSR expenditure goods and services | - |
| (g) | Goods or services for personal consumption | - |
| (h) | Goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off, given as gift or free samples | - |
| (i) | Tax paid on demands involving fraud or suppression, and on goods detained or confiscated | - |

**Plant and machinery:** the Finance Act 2025 replaced the words "plant or machinery" in section 17(5)(d) with "plant and machinery", with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. This overrides the Supreme Court's view in Safari Retreats (2024) that a building could be a "plant" under the functionality test. Plant and machinery means apparatus, equipment and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support, including the foundation; it excludes land, buildings, other civil structures, telecom towers and pipelines outside the factory.

lesson.heading: Apportionment (rules 42 and 43) and sale of capital goods
lesson.body:
Where inputs or input services are used partly for business and partly otherwise, or partly for taxable (including zero-rated) and partly for exempt supplies, section 17(1) and (2) restrict ITC.

**Rule 42 (inputs and input services), monthly:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| T | Total ITC of the month |
| T1, T2, T3 | ITC used exclusively for non-business, exclusively for exempt supplies, and blocked under 17(5) |
| C1 = T - (T1 + T2 + T3) | ITC credited to ledger |
| T4 | ITC used exclusively for taxable supplies (including zero-rated) |
| C2 = C1 - T4 | Common credit |
| D1 = (E / F) x C2 | Attributable to exempt supplies; E = exempt turnover, F = total turnover in the State |
| D2 = 5% of C2 | Attributable to non-business use (where common credit is used for non-business too) |
| C3 = C2 - (D1 + D2) | Eligible common credit |

Eligible ITC = T4 + C3. D1 and D2 are reversed. A final calculation for the year is made before the due date of the September return of the next year; excess reversal is re-claimed and short reversal is paid with interest.

**Rule 43 (capital goods):** credit on common capital goods (Tc) is spread over 60 months: Tm = Tc / 60 per month; the exempt share Te = (E / F) x Tm is reversed each month.

**Sale of capital goods (section 18(6) and rule 44(6)):** pay the **higher** of (a) ITC taken minus 5 percentage points for every quarter or part of a quarter since the invoice date, and (b) tax on the transaction value.

**Order of utilisation (section 49 and rule 88A):** IGST credit first against IGST, then against CGST and SGST in any order; CGST credit against CGST then IGST; SGST credit against SGST then IGST. CGST credit can never pay SGST, and vice versa. IGST credit must be fully used before CGST or SGST credit is used.

lesson.heading: Input Service Distributor and job work
lesson.body:
**ISD (sections 2(61) and 20, rule 39).** From **1 April 2025** ISD is **mandatory**: an office that receives invoices for input services, including services under **reverse charge** under section 9(3) and 9(4), for or on behalf of distinct persons (same PAN) must register as ISD and distribute the credit. Distribution rules:

- Credit attributable to one recipient goes only to that recipient.
- Common credit goes to recipients that use the service, in the ratio of their **turnover in the State** during the relevant period (normally the previous financial year), using C1 = (t1 / T) x C.
- Credit is distributed in the same month, through an ISD invoice, and filed in GSTR-6.
- CGST and SGST credit is distributed as CGST and SGST to a recipient in the **same State** as the ISD and as **IGST** to a recipient in **another State**. IGST is distributed as IGST.

**Job work (sections 19 and 143).** A registered principal can send inputs and capital goods to a job worker without paying tax under a delivery challan, and can take ITC even if the goods go directly from the supplier to the job worker.

| Item | Return within | Effect of failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inputs | 1 year | Deemed supplied by the principal on the date they were sent out |
| Capital goods | 3 years | Deemed supplied on the date sent out |
| Moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures, tools | No time limit | - |

Waste and scrap at the job worker's premises can be supplied by the job worker if registered, otherwise by the principal.

**Common mistakes:** blocking ITC on a truck (only passenger vehicles up to 13 seats are blocked); forgetting the 5% D2 portion in rule 42; distributing CGST to an out-of-State unit as CGST instead of IGST; and counting quarters wrongly in section 18(6) (part of a quarter counts as a full quarter).

keyPoints: Section 16(2): invoice, GSTR-2B reflection, receipt (last lot), tax paid by supplier, return filed. Pay supplier within 180 days or reverse with interest.
Section 16(4) deadline: 30 November after the financial year or annual return date, whichever is earlier.
17(5)(a): passenger motor vehicles of up to 13 seats are blocked; goods carriages are not. 17(5)(c)/(d): building blocked; plant and machinery (Finance Act 2025, retrospective) allowed.
Rule 42: eligible = T4 + C2 - D1 - D2, with D1 = E/F x C2 and D2 = 5% of C2. Rule 43: Tm = Tc/60, Te = E/F x Tm.
Section 18(6): pay higher of (ITC less 5 points per quarter or part) and tax on transaction value.
ISD mandatory from 1 April 2025, including reverse charge input services; common credit by previous year's State turnover; out-of-State share goes as IGST.
Job work: inputs back in 1 year, capital goods in 3 years; moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools exempt from the limit.

cases.title: Case: Pinnacle Retail Ltd
cases.body:
Pinnacle Retail Ltd has its head office in Mumbai, registered as an Input Service Distributor (ISD) in Maharashtra. It has three distinct registered units:

| Unit | State | Turnover in previous financial year (₹ crore) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pune store | Maharashtra | 30 |
| Ahmedabad store | Gujarat | 50 |
| Bengaluru store | Karnataka | 20 |

In February 2027 the head office received:

| Input service | GST charged |
| --- | --- |
| Brand advertising for all three units, from a Mumbai agency | CGST ₹5,00,000 + SGST ₹5,00,000 |
| IT support used only by the Bengaluru store, from a Delhi vendor | IGST ₹1,80,000 |

All units make only taxable supplies.

questions.prompt: A registered person files the annual return for 2026-27 on 15 October 2027. By when can he claim ITC on an invoice dated 10 March 2027 that he missed?
options: 30 September 2027
15 October 2027
30 November 2027
31 December 2027
questions.explanation: Section 16(4): ITC cannot be taken after 30 November following the end of the financial year, or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier. The annual return was filed on 15 October 2027, earlier than 30 November 2027.

questions.prompt: In which case is ITC on a motor vehicle allowed?
options: A 7-seater car used by the managing director for factory visits
A 5-seater car bought by a driving school for training learners
An 8-seater car used by a CA firm to take staff to client sites
Repair of a 5-seater car used by sales staff
questions.explanation: Section 17(5)(a) blocks ITC on passenger motor vehicles with seating of up to 13 persons, except when used for further supply of vehicles, transport of passengers or imparting driving training. Repairs of a blocked vehicle are blocked by 17(5)(ab).

questions.prompt: In what form does the ISD distribute the Ahmedabad store's share of the advertising credit?
options: As CGST and SGST, since the credit was CGST and SGST
As IGST, since the recipient is in a different State from the ISD
As SGST of Gujarat
It cannot be distributed, as Maharashtra SGST cannot benefit another State
questions.explanation: Rule 39: CGST and SGST credit is distributed as IGST to a recipient located in a State other than the State of the ISD. The Pune store, in Maharashtra, receives its share as CGST and SGST.

questions.prompt: What is the total credit distributed to the Bengaluru store for February 2027?
questions.explanation: Credit attributable to one unit goes only to it: IGST ₹1,80,000. Common advertising credit of ₹10,00,000 is shared by turnover: 20 / 100 x 10,00,000 = ₹2,00,000, distributed as IGST. Total ₹3,80,000.

questions.prompt: After the Finance Act 2025 amendment, a developer can claim ITC on construction of a shopping mall it will let out, by treating the building as a plant under the functionality test.
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2025 replaced "plant or machinery" with "plant and machinery" in section 17(5)(d), retrospectively from 1 July 2017. The definition of plant and machinery excludes land, buildings and civil structures, so ITC on construction of a building on own account is blocked even if it is let out.

questions.prompt: For a manufacturer, which of these input tax credits are blocked under section 17(5)?
options: GST on free samples distributed to doctors
GST on a goods truck used to deliver finished goods
GST on membership of a golf club for directors
GST on a works contract for construction of the factory building
GST on foundation work for a new machine
GST on raw material destroyed in a fire
questions.explanation: Free samples and goods destroyed (17(5)(h)), club membership (17(5)(b)(ii)) and a works contract for a building (17(5)(c)) are blocked. A goods carriage is outside 17(5)(a). The foundation of a machine is part of plant and machinery, so ITC is allowed.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: capital goods (other than moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools) sent to a job worker must be brought back within ___ years, failing which they are deemed supplied.
questions.explanation: Section 143(1)(b): capital goods within 3 years and inputs within 1 year of being sent out. Moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools have no time limit.

questions.prompt: Compute the ITC on inputs and input services that Kiran Industries can retain for the month under rule 42 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Total ITC on inputs and input services (T) | 5,00,000 |
| Used exclusively for non-business purposes (T1) | 20,000 |
| Used exclusively for exempt supplies (T2) | 30,000 |
| Blocked under section 17(5) (T3) | 50,000 |
| Used exclusively for taxable supplies (T4) | 1,50,000 |
| Exempt turnover in the State (E) | 20,00,000 |
| Total turnover in the State (F) | 1,00,00,000 |

The common credit is also used partly for non-business purposes.

questions.prompt: Compute the amount to be reversed for the month under rule 43 for the exempt use of common capital goods (round to the nearest rupee). Ignore non-business use.
questions.data: A manufacturer bought a machine used for both taxable and exempt supplies. ITC on it (Tc) is ₹6,00,000. In the month, exempt turnover is ₹25,00,000 and total turnover is ₹1,00,00,000.
questions.explanation:
| Step | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Tm = Tc / 60 = 6,00,000 / 60 | 10,000 |
| Te = E / F x Tm = 25,00,000 / 1,00,00,000 x 10,000 | 2,500 |

Te of ₹2,500 is added to output tax liability each month over the useful life of 60 months.

questions.prompt: Compute the credit distributed to the Ahmedabad store for February 2027 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.explanation:
Only the common advertising credit goes to Ahmedabad. Total turnover of recipients using it = 30 + 50 + 20 = ₹100 crore.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Common credit (CGST 5,00,000 + SGST 5,00,000) | 10,00,000 |
| Ahmedabad share 50 / 100 | 5,00,000 |

Distributed as IGST because Gujarat is a different State from the ISD.

questions.prompt: Compute the GST payable on sale of the machine (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: A registered manufacturer bought a machine on 1 April 2025 and took ITC of ₹1,80,000. It sells the machine on 15 July 2027 for ₹4,00,000 plus GST at 18%.
questions.explanation:
Section 18(6) with rule 44(6): pay the higher of the two amounts.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Quarters or part from 1 April 2025 to 15 July 2027: 9 full quarters + 1 part | 10 |
| Reduction: 10 x 5% = 50% of 1,80,000 | 90,000 |
| (a) ITC less reduction | 90,000 |
| (b) Tax on transaction value: 4,00,000 x 18% | 72,000 |
| **Payable: higher of (a) and (b)** | **90,000** |

questions.prompt: State the conditions under section 16 of the CGST Act for availing input tax credit, including the time limit and the 180-day payment rule.
questions.answer:
- **Section 16(1):** ITC is available on goods or services used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business, subject to conditions and restrictions.
- **Section 16(2):** (a) possession of a tax invoice or debit note; (aa) invoice details furnished by the supplier and communicated in GSTR-2B; (b) receipt of goods or services, including bill to ship to receipt, and receipt of the last lot when goods come in lots; (ba) ITC not restricted under section 38; (c) tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier; (d) recipient has filed his section 39 return.
- **Second proviso:** if the recipient does not pay the supplier the value and tax within 180 days of the invoice date, the ITC is added to his output tax with interest; it can be re-availed on payment. Not applicable to reverse charge.
- **Section 16(3):** no ITC on the tax component if depreciation is claimed on it under income-tax law.
- **Section 16(4):** no ITC after 30 November following the end of the financial year or the annual return date, whichever is earlier.

questions.prompt: Explain the GST provisions on sending inputs and capital goods to a job worker.
questions.answer:
- **Section 143:** a registered principal may send inputs and capital goods to a job worker under intimation and a delivery challan, without payment of tax, and bring them back or supply them from the job worker's premises (on declaration) or send them to another job worker.
- **Time limits:** inputs within 1 year and capital goods within 3 years of being sent out. Otherwise they are deemed supplied by the principal on the day they were sent out, and tax is paid with interest. Moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools are exempt from the time limit. The Commissioner can extend the limit by 1 year for inputs and 2 years for capital goods on sufficient cause.
- **Section 19:** the principal can take ITC on inputs and capital goods sent to a job worker, even when they go directly from the supplier to the job worker.
- **Waste and scrap:** may be supplied by the job worker on payment of tax if registered, or by the principal if the job worker is not registered.
- The job worker's own service is a supply of service taxed at the applicable job work rate; his turnover decides his registration.
