chapters.title: Registration, Invoicing, E-way Bill, Payment, Returns and Refunds
chapters.summary: Registration thresholds and compulsory registration, tax invoice and e-invoicing, e-way bill, payment and interest, the return cycle and refunds of zero-rated and inverted duty supplies, including the Finance Act 2026 change to provisional refund.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act and Rules as amended by Finance Act 2026 (section 54 amendment in force from 1 November 2026)

lesson.heading: Registration: sections 22 to 30
lesson.body:
**Threshold (section 22):** a supplier must register in each State from which he makes taxable supply if his **aggregate turnover** (all-India, same PAN, including exempt and export supplies, excluding GST and inward reverse charge supplies) exceeds:

| Supplier | Normal States | Special category States notified at the lower limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Services, or goods and services | ₹20 lakh | ₹10 lakh |
| Exclusively goods (where the State has adopted the higher limit; excludes notified goods such as ice cream, pan masala and tobacco) | ₹40 lakh | - |

Apply within **30 days** of becoming liable.

**Compulsory registration regardless of turnover (section 24):** inter-State taxable supply of goods; casual taxable persons; persons liable under reverse charge; e-commerce operators required to collect TCS; non-resident taxable persons; persons deducting TDS under section 51; ISDs; agents supplying on behalf of others; persons supplying OIDAR services from outside India to unregistered persons in India; and persons supplying goods through an e-commerce operator (except small suppliers notified for intra-State supplies). Inter-State **services** up to the threshold are exempted from compulsory registration by notification.

**Casual and non-resident taxable persons (section 27):** apply at least 5 days before starting business; registration valid for the period stated or **90 days**, extendable by up to 90 days; advance deposit of estimated tax.

**Cancellation (section 29) and revocation (section 30):** application for revocation within 90 days of the cancellation order (extendable by a further 180 days).

lesson.heading: Tax invoice, e-invoicing and e-way bill
lesson.body:
**Tax invoice (section 31):** goods: before or at the time of removal (or delivery where no removal). Services: within **30 days** of supply (45 days for banks, insurers and NBFCs). Continuous supply follows the contract terms. HSN codes on invoices: 4 digits for aggregate turnover up to ₹5 crore in the previous year, 6 digits above.

**E-invoicing (rule 48(4)):** mandatory for B2B invoices, credit and debit notes and exports where aggregate turnover in **any financial year from 2017-18** exceeded **₹5 crore**. The invoice is uploaded to the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), which returns an Invoice Reference Number (IRN) and a signed QR code. An invoice without an IRN is not a valid invoice (rule 48(5)). Taxpayers with aggregate turnover of **₹10 crore or more** cannot report an invoice to the IRP more than **30 days** after its date. Exempt from e-invoicing: SEZ units, insurers, banks and NBFCs, GTAs, passenger transport, cinema admission and Government departments.

**E-way bill (rule 138):** needed for movement of goods of consignment value above **₹50,000** (value including GST, excluding exempt goods), whether or not for supply. Part A has invoice and goods details; Part B has vehicle details.

| Cargo | Validity |
| --- | --- |
| Normal cargo | 1 day for every 200 km or part |
| Over dimensional cargo | 1 day for every 20 km or part |

A day ends at midnight of the following day after generation. Validity can be extended within 8 hours before or after expiry. No e-way bill is needed for notified goods (for example fresh vegetables), non-motorised conveyance, goods moving from port or customs station to an ICD under customs seal, and movement within a notified distance for weighment.

lesson.heading: Payment, interest and returns
lesson.body:
**Ledgers (section 49):** electronic cash ledger, electronic credit ledger and electronic liability register. Reverse charge tax, interest, penalty and late fee are paid in cash.

**Order of ITC utilisation (rule 88A):** IGST credit first against IGST, then CGST and SGST in any order; CGST credit against CGST then IGST; SGST credit against SGST then IGST; never CGST against SGST.

**Rule 86B:** a person whose taxable supply in a month exceeds ₹50 lakh cannot use credit for more than 99% of output tax, subject to exceptions (for example, income tax paid above ₹1 lakh in each of the last 2 years, or refunds above ₹1 lakh).

**Interest (section 50):** 18% per annum on tax paid late, on the **net cash liability** where the return is filed late (unless filed after a notice). Interest on ITC wrongly availed **and utilised** is 18% from the date of utilisation (rule 88B). Calculation: tax x 18% x days / 365.

**Return cycle:**

| Return | Content | Due date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GSTR-1 | Outward supplies | 11th of next month; quarterly by 13th under QRMP |
| IFF | B2B invoices for the first 2 months of a quarter (QRMP) | 13th of next month |
| GSTR-3B | Summary return and payment | 20th of next month; 22nd or 24th for QRMP filers (by State) |
| GSTR-9 | Annual return | 31 December following the year; optional for turnover up to ₹2 crore |
| GSTR-9C | Self-certified reconciliation | With GSTR-9, for turnover above ₹5 crore |

QRMP is available to taxpayers with aggregate turnover up to ₹5 crore. GSTR-2B is a static auto-drafted ITC statement that drives ITC eligibility.

lesson.heading: Refunds: section 54 and rule 89
lesson.body:
Refund must be claimed within **2 years from the relevant date** (for export of goods: date the ship or aircraft leaves India; for services: date of receipt of payment or invoice, as applicable; for inverted duty: due date of the return for the period). Minimum refund ₹1,000. The order is due within **60 days** of a complete application; delayed refund carries interest at 6% (9% where it follows an appellate order) under section 56.

**Zero-rated supply under LUT (rule 89(4)):**

Refund = (Turnover of zero-rated supply x Net ITC) / Adjusted total turnover

**Inverted duty structure (section 54(3)(ii), rule 89(5)):**

Maximum refund = (Turnover of inverted rated supply x Net ITC / Adjusted total turnover) - (Tax payable on such inverted rated supply x Net ITC / ITC availed on inputs and input services)

Net ITC here means ITC on **inputs** only, not input services or capital goods.

**Provisional refund (section 54(6)):** 90% of the claim is granted provisionally for zero-rated supplies. The **Finance Act 2026** (in force from **1 November 2026**) extends provisional refund to refunds arising from an **inverted duty structure**.

**Worked example (inverted duty).** Turnover of inverted rated supply and adjusted total turnover ₹1,00,00,000; tax payable on it ₹5,00,000; Net ITC ₹12,00,000; ITC on inputs and input services ₹13,00,000.

| Step | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 1,00,00,000 x 12,00,000 / 1,00,00,000 | 12,00,000 |
| Less: 5,00,000 x 12,00,000 / 13,00,000 | (4,61,538) |
| **Maximum refund** | **7,38,462** |

**Common mistakes:** including input services in Net ITC for inverted refund; using the e-way bill validity of 100 km per day (it is 200 km); charging interest on gross liability instead of net cash liability; and forgetting that reverse charge tax cannot be paid through ITC.

keyPoints: Registration threshold: ₹20 lakh (₹10 lakh in notified special category States); ₹40 lakh for exclusive goods suppliers where adopted. Apply within 30 days.
Section 24 compulsory registration: inter-State goods, casual and non-resident persons, reverse charge recipients, ISD, TDS deductors, e-commerce cases.
E-invoicing: aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore in any year since 2017-18; turnover ₹10 crore or more must report to IRP within 30 days.
E-way bill above ₹50,000; validity 1 day per 200 km (20 km for over dimensional cargo).
Interest 18% on net cash liability; rule 88B for wrongly availed and utilised ITC. GSTR-3B 20th, GSTR-1 11th, GSTR-9 31 December.
Refund within 2 years; rule 89(4) for zero-rated, rule 89(5) for inverted duty (Net ITC on inputs only). Provisional 90% refund extended to inverted duty from 1 November 2026.

cases.title: Case: Lumen Electronics Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
Lumen Electronics Pvt Ltd, Noida (Uttar Pradesh), had aggregate turnover of ₹12 crore in 2025-26. It files monthly returns. Events in early 2027:

- A B2B invoice dated 5 January 2027 was not reported to the IRP. The accounts team tries to report it on 20 February 2027.
- On 10 February 2027 it sends a consignment worth ₹4,50,000 (including GST) to a buyer in Pune by road. The road distance is 1,450 km. The goods are normal cargo.
- GSTR-3B for December 2026 (due 20 January 2027) was filed and the tax paid on 1 March 2027. Its net tax payable in cash for December was ₹2,00,000; the rest was set off against ITC.

questions.prompt: Anand runs a consultancy only in Karnataka, supplying only intra-State services. Above what aggregate turnover must he register?
options: ₹10 lakh
₹20 lakh
₹40 lakh
₹1.5 crore
questions.explanation: Section 22: the threshold is ₹20 lakh for service providers in States other than the notified special category States (₹10 lakh). The ₹40 lakh limit is only for suppliers exclusively of goods. ₹1.5 crore is the composition limit.

questions.prompt: A CA firm completes a due diligence assignment on 4 March. By when must it issue the tax invoice under section 31 read with rule 47?
options: 4 March
Within 15 days
Within 30 days
Within 45 days
questions.explanation: A tax invoice for services must be issued within 30 days of the date of supply. The 45-day limit applies only to insurers, banking companies, financial institutions and NBFCs.

questions.prompt: What is the status of the 5 January 2027 invoice that Lumen tries to report on 20 February 2027?
options: It can be reported, as there is no time limit for IRP reporting
It cannot be reported, as Lumen's turnover is ₹10 crore or more and 30 days have passed; without an IRN it is not a valid invoice
It can be reported with a late fee of ₹50 per day
E-invoicing does not apply because turnover is below ₹20 crore
questions.explanation: E-invoicing applies above ₹5 crore. Taxpayers with aggregate turnover of ₹10 crore or more cannot report an invoice to the IRP after 30 days from its date. An invoice without an IRN is not valid under rule 48(5), so Lumen must issue a fresh invoice and the buyer's ITC is at risk until it does.

questions.prompt: What is the validity of the e-way bill for the Noida to Pune consignment?
options: 5 days
7 days
8 days
15 days
questions.explanation: Normal cargo: 1 day for every 200 km or part. 1,450 / 200 = 7.25, so 7 full blocks plus a part: 8 days. The consignment value exceeds ₹50,000, so an e-way bill is required.

questions.prompt: A casual taxable person's registration is valid for the period specified in the application or 90 days, whichever is earlier, and can be extended.
questions.explanation: Section 27(1): the certificate is valid for the period specified or 90 days from the effective date, whichever is earlier, and the proper officer can extend it by up to 90 days on request. The person must also deposit estimated tax in advance.

questions.prompt: Which of these persons must register under section 24 even if their aggregate turnover is below the threshold?
options: A trader making inter-State supply of goods
A person liable to pay tax under reverse charge
A casual taxable person making taxable supply
An Input Service Distributor
A person making only exempt intra-State supplies
questions.explanation: Section 24 lists inter-State suppliers of goods, reverse charge recipients, casual taxable persons and ISDs, among others. A person making only exempt supplies is not liable to register (section 23).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: an e-way bill is required where the consignment value exceeds ₹___.
questions.explanation: Rule 138(1): movement of goods of consignment value above ₹50,000. Consignment value includes GST and excludes the value of exempt goods in the same invoice.

questions.prompt: Compute the refund of unutilised ITC on export of goods under LUT under rule 89(4) (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Turnover of zero-rated supply of goods (under LUT) | 60,00,000 |
| Turnover of domestic taxable supply | 40,00,000 |
| Adjusted total turnover | 1,00,00,000 |
| Net ITC for the period | 9,00,000 |
questions.explanation: Refund = Turnover of zero-rated supply x Net ITC / Adjusted total turnover = 60,00,000 x 9,00,000 / 1,00,00,000 = ₹5,40,000.

questions.prompt: Compute the maximum refund under rule 89(5) for an inverted duty structure (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data:
A manufacturer buys inputs at 18% and sells its output at 5%.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Turnover of inverted rated supply | 1,00,00,000 |
| Adjusted total turnover | 1,00,00,000 |
| Tax payable on the inverted rated supply | 5,00,000 |
| ITC on inputs (Net ITC) | 12,00,000 |
| ITC on input services | 1,00,000 |
questions.explanation:
| Step | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| A = 1,00,00,000 x 12,00,000 / 1,00,00,000 | 12,00,000 |
| ITC on inputs and input services = 12,00,000 + 1,00,000 | 13,00,000 |
| B = 5,00,000 x 12,00,000 / 13,00,000 | 4,61,538 |
| **Maximum refund = A - B** | **7,38,462** |

Input service credit is excluded from Net ITC but included in the denominator of the second term.

questions.prompt: Compute the interest payable by Lumen under section 50 on the late payment for December 2026 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.explanation:
Interest runs on the net cash liability (the return was filed late but not after a notice) from the day after the due date to the date of payment.

| Particulars | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Days: 21-31 January (11) + February 2027 (28) + 1 March (1) | 40 |
| Interest = 2,00,000 x 18% x 40 / 365 | ₹3,945 |

questions.prompt: What is the time limit for claiming a refund of tax under section 54(1)?
options: 1 year from the relevant date
2 years from the relevant date
3 years from the end of the financial year
60 days from the date of export
questions.explanation: Section 54(1): the application must be made before the expiry of 2 years from the relevant date. The relevant date depends on the type of refund (explanation 2 to section 54).

questions.prompt: Compute the minimum cash payment for the month by Sagar Industries, showing the ITC set-off under section 49 and rule 88A.
questions.data:
| Head | Output tax (forward charge) (₹) | ITC available (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IGST | 2,00,000 | 2,80,000 |
| CGST | 1,50,000 | 60,000 |
| SGST | 1,50,000 | 1,00,000 |

In addition, tax under reverse charge on legal services is CGST ₹9,000 and SGST ₹9,000. Rule 86B does not apply.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: IGST credit first (rule 88A).**

| Use of IGST credit 2,80,000 | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Against IGST liability | 2,00,000 |
| Balance against CGST (any split between CGST and SGST is allowed) | 80,000 |

**Step 2: CGST and SGST credit.**

| Head | Liability (₹) | IGST credit (₹) | Own credit (₹) | Cash (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IGST | 2,00,000 | 2,00,000 | - | Nil |
| CGST | 1,50,000 | 80,000 | 60,000 | 10,000 |
| SGST | 1,50,000 | - | 1,00,000 | 50,000 |
| **Forward charge cash** | | | | **60,000** |

**Step 3: reverse charge in cash.** CGST 9,000 + SGST 9,000 = 18,000.

**Total cash payment = ₹78,000** (CGST ₹19,000, SGST ₹59,000). Whatever split of the ₹80,000 IGST credit is chosen, total cash stays ₹60,000 for forward charge because CGST credit cannot pay SGST and vice versa.

questions.prompt: Explain the e-invoicing system under GST: applicability, the process, exemptions and the consequence of not generating an IRN.
questions.answer:
- **Applicability:** rule 48(4) requires registered persons whose aggregate turnover in any financial year from 2017-18 exceeded ₹5 crore to prepare B2B invoices, credit and debit notes, and export invoices through the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP).
- **Process:** the supplier uploads invoice details in the prescribed schema; the IRP validates them, generates an Invoice Reference Number (IRN), digitally signs the invoice and returns a QR code. Data flows to GSTR-1 and the e-way bill system.
- **Time limit:** taxpayers with aggregate turnover of ₹10 crore or more must report within 30 days of the invoice date.
- **Exemptions:** SEZ units, insurers, banks, financial institutions and NBFCs, GTAs, passenger transport, cinema admission, and Government departments and local authorities.
- **Consequence:** an invoice without an IRN is not a valid tax invoice (rule 48(5)); the recipient cannot take ITC on it, and penalty under section 122 can apply for not issuing a proper invoice.

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions for refund of unutilised ITC under section 54(3), including the formula for inverted duty refund and the Finance Act 2026 change to provisional refund.
questions.answer:
- **Section 54(3):** refund of unutilised ITC is allowed only in two cases: (i) zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax (under LUT), and (ii) where ITC accumulates because the rate on inputs is higher than on output supplies (inverted duty), other than nil-rated or fully exempt supplies and notified goods or services.
- **Zero-rated (rule 89(4)):** refund = turnover of zero-rated supply x Net ITC / adjusted total turnover.
- **Inverted duty (rule 89(5)):** maximum refund = (turnover of inverted rated supply x Net ITC / adjusted total turnover) - (tax payable on such supply x Net ITC / ITC availed on inputs and input services). Net ITC means ITC on inputs only.
- **Time limit:** 2 years from the relevant date; order within 60 days; interest at 6% under section 56 for delay.
- **Provisional refund (section 54(6)):** 90% of a zero-rated refund claim is granted provisionally. The Finance Act 2026, in force from 1 November 2026, extends provisional refund to inverted duty claims, which improves working capital for such manufacturers.
- Unjust enrichment does not apply to refunds of ITC under these provisions.

chapters.title: Assessment, Audit, Search, Demands, Recovery and Penalties
chapters.summary: Types of assessment, departmental and special audit, inspection, search, seizure and detention, the demand provisions including section 74A for 2024-25 onwards, recovery, and offences and penalties.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Assessment and audit
lesson.body:
| Section | Type | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 59 | Self-assessment | Every registered person assesses his own tax in the return |
| 60 | Provisional | On request, when value or rate cannot be determined; bond with security; final assessment within 6 months (extendable) |
| 61 | Scrutiny of returns | Discrepancies notified (ASMT-10); explanation within 30 days; action under section 65, 66, 67, 73, 74 or 74A if not resolved |
| 62 | Best judgment, non-filers | After notice under section 46; order within 5 years of the due date of the annual return; **deemed withdrawn** if a valid return is filed within 60 days of the order |
| 63 | Unregistered or cancelled persons | Best judgment within 5 years of the due date of the annual return |
| 64 | Summary | To protect revenue, with Additional or Joint Commissioner's permission, where delay would harm revenue |

**Audit:**

- **Section 65, departmental audit:** by the Commissioner or an authorised officer; at least **15 working days** notice; completed within **3 months**, extendable by up to 6 months; findings in ADT-02 within 30 days.
- **Section 66, special audit:** ordered by an Assistant Commissioner with Commissioner's approval, at any stage of scrutiny, inquiry or investigation, where the value is not correctly declared or credit availed is not within normal limits. Done by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by the Commissioner; report within **90 days**, extendable by 90 days. The taxpayer is heard on the findings.

The mandatory audit by a CA under old section 35(5) was omitted in 2021; GSTR-9C is now self-certified.

lesson.heading: Inspection, search, seizure, detention and arrest
lesson.body:
**Section 67:** a Joint Commissioner or above, with reasons to believe that a person has suppressed transactions, claimed excess ITC or contravened the law, can authorise **inspection** of places of business. Where goods liable to confiscation or relevant documents are hidden, he can authorise **search and seizure**. Seized goods are returned if no notice is issued within **6 months** (extendable by 6 months). Seized goods can be released provisionally on a bond and security.

**Section 129, detention of goods in transit:** goods or conveyances moved in contravention (for example without an e-way bill) are released on payment of penalty:

| Situation | Taxable goods | Exempt goods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner comes forward | 200% of tax payable | 2% of value or ₹25,000, whichever is less |
| Owner does not come forward | 50% of value or 200% of tax, whichever is higher | 5% of value or ₹25,000, whichever is less |

The Finance Act 2023 delinked section 129 from confiscation under section 130. If the penalty is not paid within 15 days of the order, the goods can be sold to recover it.

**Section 69, arrest:** the Commissioner can authorise arrest for offences under section 132(1)(a) to (d) (supply without invoice, fake invoices, wrongful ITC, collecting tax and not paying it) when the amount exceeds **₹5 crore** (cognizable and non-bailable) or ₹2 crore or more (non-cognizable and bailable).

lesson.heading: Demands: sections 73, 74 and 74A
lesson.body:
Sections 73 (non-fraud) and 74 (fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression) apply to demands for **financial years up to 2023-24**. **Section 74A** applies to demands for **2024-25 onwards** and uses one time limit for both kinds of cases.

| Point | Section 74A |
| --- | --- |
| Show cause notice (SCN) | Within **42 months** from the due date of the annual return for the year (or the date of erroneous refund) |
| Order | Within **12 months** from the SCN, extendable by up to 6 months |
| Minimum | No SCN if tax is less than ₹1,000 |
| Penalty, non-fraud | 10% of tax or ₹10,000, whichever is higher |
| Penalty, fraud or suppression | Equal to the tax |

**Reduced penalty under section 74A:**

| When tax and interest are paid | Non-fraud | Fraud |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before SCN | No penalty | 15% of tax |
| Within 60 days of SCN | No penalty, proceedings closed | 25% of tax |
| Within 60 days of the order | Normal penalty | 50% of tax |
| Later | Normal penalty | 100% of tax |

For comparison, old section 73 required the order within 3 years of the annual return due date (SCN at least 3 months before) and section 74 within 5 years (SCN at least 6 months before). Section 128A waived interest and penalty on section 73 demands for 2017-18 to 2019-20 if the tax was paid by the notified date.

**Worked example.** For 2025-26 (annual return due 31 December 2026), the SCN deadline under section 74A is 42 months later: 30 June 2030.

lesson.heading: Recovery, offences and penalties
lesson.body:
**Recovery (sections 78 to 84):** amount payable under an order must be paid within **3 months** (shorter if the officer records reasons). Modes under section 79: deduction from money owed to the defaulter by the department; detention and sale of goods; garnishee notice to third parties who owe him money; distraint and sale of movable or immovable property; recovery as arrears of land revenue; and through a Magistrate. **Section 80:** payment in up to 24 monthly instalments. **Section 83:** provisional attachment of property, including bank accounts, valid for 1 year. Transferee of a business (85), directors of a private company (89) and partners (90) can be held liable.

**Penalties:**

| Section | Penalty |
| --- | --- |
| 122(1) | ₹10,000 or the tax evaded, ITC wrongly availed or refund wrongly claimed, whichever is higher, for 21 listed offences (for example supply without invoice, fake invoices) |
| 122(1A) | A person who retains the benefit of and causes certain offences: penalty equal to tax or ITC involved |
| 122(2) | Non-fraud short payment: ₹10,000 or 10% of tax; fraud: ₹10,000 or tax, higher in each case |
| 125 | General penalty up to ₹25,000 where no penalty is specified |
| 126 | No penalty for minor breaches (tax involved under ₹5,000) or easily rectifiable mistakes without fraudulent intent; reasons must be recorded and the person heard |

**Prosecution (section 132):** imprisonment depends on the amount (up to 5 years above ₹5 crore). Prosecution is launched only with the Commissioner's sanction, and offences can be compounded under section 138 after the person pays tax, interest and penalty.

**Common mistakes:** applying section 73 time limits to 2024-25 demands; giving "no penalty" in a fraud case paid before SCN (it is 15%); and treating section 129 penalty as tax plus penalty.

keyPoints: Section 62 best judgment order is deemed withdrawn if a valid return is filed within 60 days.
Section 65 audit: 15 working days notice, complete in 3 months (+6). Section 66 special audit: CA or CMA, report in 90 days (+90).
Section 67: Joint Commissioner authorises; seized goods returned if no notice in 6 months (+6). Section 69 arrest above ₹5 crore (cognizable, non-bailable).
Section 129 penalty: 200% of tax (owner comes forward); higher of 50% of value or 200% of tax (owner does not).
Section 74A (2024-25 on): SCN in 42 months, order in 12 months; penalty 10% or ₹10,000 (non-fraud), 100% (fraud); fraud reduced to 15% / 25% / 50%.
Recovery within 3 months; section 79 modes; up to 24 instalments; provisional attachment valid 1 year.

cases.title: Case: Swift Agro Traders
cases.body:
Swift Agro Traders, Indore, is a registered dealer. A departmental audit under section 65 of its records for 2024-25 (annual return due date 31 December 2025) found:

| Issue | Nature | Tax short paid (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Wrong classification of a product at 5% instead of 18%; no intent to evade | 60,000 |
| B | ITC taken on invoices of a non-existent supplier, with knowledge | 8,00,000 |

Interest is to be computed separately. The department intends to proceed under section 74A.

questions.prompt: A non-filer receives a best judgment assessment order under section 62 on 1 March. He files a valid return on 20 April. What happens to the order?
options: It remains, and he must appeal against it
It is deemed withdrawn, though interest and late fee remain payable
It is reduced by 50%
It is withdrawn only if the Commissioner agrees
questions.explanation: Section 62(2): if a valid return is furnished within 60 days of service of the assessment order, the order is deemed withdrawn. Liability for interest under section 50 and late fee under section 47 continues.

questions.prompt: Who conducts a special audit under section 66?
options: A departmental audit team under the Commissioner
A chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by the Commissioner
The statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act
Any chartered accountant chosen by the taxpayer
questions.explanation: Section 66(1): the Assistant Commissioner, with prior approval of the Commissioner, directs the registered person to get records audited by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by the Commissioner. The report is due within 90 days, extendable by 90 days.

questions.prompt: By what date must the show cause notice under section 74A for 2024-25 be issued?
options: 31 December 2027
30 September 2028
30 June 2029
31 December 2030
questions.explanation: Section 74A(2): SCN within 42 months from the due date of the annual return for the financial year. 31 December 2025 plus 42 months = 30 June 2029. The same limit applies to fraud and non-fraud cases.

questions.prompt: If Swift pays the tax of ₹60,000 on issue A with interest within 60 days of the SCN, what penalty applies?
options: No penalty; proceedings for issue A are concluded
questions.explanation: Issue A is a non-fraud case. Under section 74A, where tax and interest are paid within 60 days of the SCN in a non-fraud case, no penalty is payable and the proceedings are deemed concluded.

questions.prompt: Offences under section 132(1)(a) to (d) involving more than ₹5 crore are cognizable and non-bailable.
questions.explanation: Section 132(5): offences under clauses (a) to (d) of section 132(1) are cognizable and non-bailable where the amount exceeds ₹5 crore. Other offences are non-cognizable and bailable.

questions.prompt: Which of these are modes of recovery available to the proper officer under section 79?
options: Deducting the amount from money owed by the department to the defaulter
Garnishee notice to the defaulter's customer who owes him money
Distraint and sale of the defaulter's movable property
Recovery as arrears of land revenue through the Collector
Cancelling the PAN of the defaulter
questions.explanation: Section 79 provides deduction, detention and sale of goods, garnishee notice, distraint and sale of property, recovery as land revenue and recovery through a Magistrate. PAN is under the Income-tax law and cannot be cancelled under GST.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a departmental audit under section 65 must be completed within ___ months of its commencement, unless extended.
questions.explanation: Section 65(4): within 3 months from commencement, extendable by the Commissioner by up to 6 months for reasons recorded in writing.

questions.prompt: Compute the total amount (tax + interest + penalty) the taxpayer must pay to conclude the proceedings (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: A show cause notice under section 74A for 2025-26 alleges suppression of sales with intent to evade tax. Tax ₹10,00,000; interest up to the date of payment ₹1,50,000. The taxpayer pays within 60 days of the SCN.
questions.explanation:
Fraud case paid within 60 days of SCN: penalty is 25% of tax.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Tax | 10,00,000 |
| Interest | 1,50,000 |
| Penalty 25% of tax | 2,50,000 |
| **Total** | **14,00,000** |

questions.prompt: Compute the penalty payable for release of the goods under section 129 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: Goods worth ₹5,00,000, taxable at 18%, are detained in transit because no e-way bill was carried. The owner of the goods does not come forward; the transporter seeks release.
questions.explanation:
Section 129(1)(b), owner not coming forward: penalty is the higher of 50% of the value of goods or 200% of the tax payable.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 50% of 5,00,000 | 2,50,000 |
| 200% of tax (18% of 5,00,000 = 90,000) | 1,80,000 |
| **Penalty (higher)** | **2,50,000** |

If the owner came forward, the penalty would be ₹1,80,000.

questions.prompt: If Swift does not pay anything on issue A and the order confirms the demand, what penalty applies to issue A under section 74A (round to the nearest rupee)?
questions.explanation: Non-fraud penalty under section 74A is 10% of tax or ₹10,000, whichever is higher. 10% of ₹60,000 = ₹6,000, so the penalty is ₹10,000.

questions.prompt: If Swift pays the tax of ₹8,00,000 on issue B with interest before the SCN is issued, what penalty must it pay?
options: Nil
questions.explanation: Issue B involves fraud. Under section 74A, a fraud case settled before the SCN carries a penalty of 15% of tax: 15% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. Only non-fraud cases settled before or within 60 days of the SCN escape penalty.

questions.prompt: For the fraud demand below, compute the total payable under section 74A at each stage of payment, and state the benefit of early payment.
questions.data: Demand under section 74A for 2025-26: ITC availed on fake invoices ₹12,00,000; interest ₹2,16,000 (assume the same interest at each stage for comparison).
questions.answer:
| Stage of payment | Penalty rate | Penalty (₹) | Tax + interest (₹) | Total (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before SCN | 15% | 1,80,000 | 14,16,000 | 15,96,000 |
| Within 60 days of SCN | 25% | 3,00,000 | 14,16,000 | 17,16,000 |
| Within 60 days of the order | 50% | 6,00,000 | 14,16,000 | 20,16,000 |
| After that | 100% | 12,00,000 | 14,16,000 | 26,16,000 |

Paying before the SCN saves ₹10,20,000 in penalty compared with the full penalty. In practice interest grows with time, so the gap is larger. Payment before SCN is made through DRC-03 with intimation; the officer then issues no notice for the amount paid. The person may still face prosecution under section 132 for fake invoices, since penalty settlement does not bar prosecution.

questions.prompt: Explain section 74A of the CGST Act: its applicability, time limits and penalty structure.
questions.answer:
- **Applicability:** demands for tax not paid, short paid, erroneously refunded, or ITC wrongly availed or utilised, for financial year **2024-25 onwards**, whether or not involving fraud. Sections 73 and 74 continue for earlier years.
- **Time limits:** SCN within 42 months from the due date of the annual return for the year (or from the date of erroneous refund); order within 12 months from the SCN, extendable by up to 6 months by a senior officer. No SCN if tax is under ₹1,000.
- **Penalty, non-fraud:** 10% of tax or ₹10,000, whichever is higher; nil if tax and interest are paid before SCN or within 60 days of it.
- **Penalty, fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression:** equal to tax; reduced to 15% if paid before SCN, 25% within 60 days of SCN, and 50% within 60 days of the order.
- **Benefit:** one time limit for both kinds of cases ends the dispute over whether the extended period was correctly invoked; the fraud finding now affects only the penalty.

questions.prompt: Explain the powers of inspection, search and seizure under section 67 of the CGST Act.
questions.answer:
- **Inspection (67(1)):** an officer not below Joint Commissioner, who has reasons to believe that a taxable person has suppressed transactions or stock, claimed excess ITC, or contravened the Act to evade tax, or that a transporter or warehouse keeper holds goods that escaped tax, can authorise inspection of any place of business.
- **Search and seizure (67(2)):** where goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things useful for proceedings, are secreted in any place, he can authorise search and seizure. Where seizure is not practicable, a prohibitory order can be served.
- **Return:** documents are retained only as long as needed; seized goods are returned if no notice is issued within 6 months, extendable by 6 months.
- **Provisional release:** on a bond and security, as prescribed.
- **Perishable or hazardous goods** can be disposed of after seizure.
- Searches follow the Code of Criminal Procedure (now the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) procedure for searches, and the person can take copies of seized documents except where it would prejudice the investigation.

chapters.title: Appeals, Revision, Advance Ruling and Liability in Certain Cases
chapters.summary: The appeal ladder from the Appellate Authority to the GST Appellate Tribunal, High Court and Supreme Court, pre-deposit, revision, the advance ruling mechanism and liability of transferees, directors, partners and legal representatives.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: The appeal ladder and pre-deposit
lesson.body:
| Forum | Section | Who files and time limit | Pre-deposit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appellate Authority (Commissioner (Appeals) or Joint/Additional Commissioner (Appeals)) | 107 | Aggrieved person: **3 months** from communication of the order, condonable by 1 month. Department: 6 months | Full admitted tax, interest, fine, fee and penalty **plus 10% of the disputed tax**, capped at **₹20 crore** each under CGST and SGST |
| GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) | 109, 112 | 3 months from the order (or from the date notified for the Tribunal's start); cross-objections within 45 days | Admitted amount **plus a further 10% of the remaining tax in dispute**, capped at **₹20 crore** each under CGST and SGST, in addition to the first-stage deposit |
| High Court | 117 | 180 days, only on a **substantial question of law**, against State Bench orders | - |
| Supreme Court | 118 | Against Principal Bench orders and High Court judgments | - |

Pre-deposit is on **tax** in dispute; interest and penalty linked to the disputed tax are not part of the 10%. For IGST, the caps are doubled (IGST Act section 20). On paying the pre-deposit, recovery of the balance is stayed. The Finance Act 2025 provides that for an appeal against an order demanding **only penalty** (no tax), the pre-deposit is 10% of the penalty.

The Principal Bench of GSTAT in New Delhi hears appeals where **place of supply** is an issue; State Benches hear the rest. GSTAT may refuse to admit an appeal where the tax, ITC, fine, fee or penalty involved does not exceed ₹50,000.

**Powers of the Appellate Authority (section 107(11)):** it can confirm, modify or annul the order but **cannot remand** the case back. It can enhance a demand or reduce a refund after a show cause notice. It should decide within 1 year where possible.

lesson.heading: Revision and non-appealable orders
lesson.body:
**Revision (section 108):** the Revisional Authority can call for records and revise an order of a subordinate officer that is erroneous and prejudicial to revenue, after hearing the person. Bars: the order is under appeal; the appeal time has not expired (or, for an order that went to appeal, more than 1 year has not passed after the appellate order); or more than **3 years** have passed since the order.

**Section 121 (non-appealable orders):** orders transferring proceedings between officers, orders seizing or retaining books, sanctioning prosecution, and orders under section 80 (instalments) cannot be appealed.

**Section 120:** the Board can fix monetary limits below which the department will not file appeals; the department's non-filing in one case does not bar it in another case on the same issue.

**Worked example (timeline).** Order communicated on 10 January 2027. First appeal due by 10 April 2027; condonable to 10 May 2027. If the Appellate Authority's order comes on 30 September 2027, appeal to GSTAT by 30 December 2027 (3 months).

lesson.heading: Advance ruling: sections 95 to 106
Liability to pay in certain cases: sections 85 to 94
lesson.body:
| Section | Situation | Liability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 85 | Transfer of business (sale, gift, lease) | Transferor and transferee jointly and severally liable for tax up to the date of transfer; transferee liable thereafter and must amend registration |
| 86 | Agent supplies on behalf of a principal | Agent and principal jointly and severally liable |
| 87 | Amalgamation or merger by court or tribunal order | Transactions between the companies from the effective date to the order date are included in their turnover; companies treated as distinct until the order date |
| 88 | Company in liquidation | Liquidator to intimate within 30 days of appointment; Commissioner to notify dues within 3 months; directors jointly liable if dues cannot be recovered, unless no gross neglect or breach of duty |
| 89 | Private company | Directors jointly and severally liable for tax that cannot be recovered from the company, unless the non-recovery is not due to their gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty |
| 90 | Partnership firm | Partners jointly and severally liable; a retiring partner is liable up to the retirement date if intimation is given within 1 month |
| 91, 92 | Guardians, trustees, Court of Wards | Liable as the person they represent |
| 93 | Death of a person | If the business is continued by the legal representative: he is liable for all dues. If discontinued: liable to the extent of the estate |
| 94 | Firm, HUF or AOP whose business is discontinued or dissolved | Every person who was a partner, member or karta is jointly and severally liable |

**Common mistakes:** including penalty in the 10% pre-deposit base; letting the Appellate Authority remand a case; asking an AAR about place of supply; and treating directors of a public company as liable under section 89 (it applies to private companies).

keyPoints: First appeal (107): 3 months + 1 month condonation; pre-deposit admitted amount + 10% of disputed tax, max ₹20 crore CGST and ₹20 crore SGST.
GSTAT (112): 3 months; further 10% of remaining disputed tax, max ₹20 crore each; Principal Bench for place of supply cases.
High Court (117): 180 days, substantial question of law. Appellate Authority cannot remand (107(11)).
Revision (108): within 3 years of the order; not while an appeal is pending.
Advance ruling: 7 questions in 97(2), no place of supply; ruling in 90 days; appeal to AAAR in 30 days; binding only on applicant and jurisdictional officer.
Section 85 transferor and transferee jointly liable; section 89 private company directors liable unless no gross neglect; section 93 legal representative.

cases.title: Case: Meghna Textiles Ltd
cases.body:
Meghna Textiles Ltd, Surat, received an order on 10 January 2027 confirming:

| Item | CGST (₹) | SGST (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tax | 40,00,000 | 40,00,000 |
| Interest | 9,00,000 | 9,00,000 |
| Penalty | 40,00,000 | 40,00,000 |

Meghna disputes the entire demand. On first appeal, the Appellate Authority's order dated 30 September 2027 drops part of the tax and confirms tax of ₹30,00,000 CGST and ₹30,00,000 SGST, with proportionate interest and penalty. Meghna decides to appeal to the GST Appellate Tribunal against the full confirmed amount.

questions.prompt: On which question can an applicant NOT seek an advance ruling under section 97(2)?
options: Classification of a product
Whether a particular activity is a supply
Place of supply of a service
Admissibility of input tax credit
questions.explanation: Section 97(2) lists classification, applicability of notifications, time and value of supply, admissibility of ITC, liability to pay tax, registration and whether an activity is a supply. Place of supply is excluded because the AAR is a State-level body and place of supply decides the tax between States.

questions.prompt: Within what period must the Authority for Advance Ruling pronounce its ruling?
options: 30 days of the application
60 days of the application
90 days of the application
6 months of the application
questions.explanation: Section 98(6): the AAR pronounces its ruling in writing within 90 days from the date of receipt of the application. The AAAR also has 90 days from the filing of an appeal.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum pre-deposit Meghna must make to file the first appeal against the 10 January 2027 order?
questions.explanation: Section 107(6): admitted amount (nil here) plus 10% of the tax in dispute. Disputed tax = 40,00,000 + 40,00,000 = ₹80,00,000; 10% = ₹8,00,000 (₹4,00,000 CGST and ₹4,00,000 SGST). Interest and penalty are not part of the base, and the ₹20 crore caps are not reached.

questions.prompt: By when must Meghna file its first appeal, without seeking condonation of delay?
options: 9 February 2027
10 March 2027
10 April 2027
10 July 2027
questions.explanation: Section 107(1): within 3 months from the date of communication of the order. From 10 January 2027 that is 10 April 2027. The Appellate Authority can condone a further delay of up to 1 month for sufficient cause (section 107(4)).

questions.prompt: The Appellate Authority under section 107 can set aside an order and remand the case to the adjudicating authority for fresh adjudication.
questions.explanation: Section 107(11): after inquiry, the Appellate Authority passes an order confirming, modifying or annulling the decision, but it cannot refer the case back to the adjudicating authority. It must decide the matter itself.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about advance rulings are correct?
options: A ruling binds the applicant and the jurisdictional officer for the applicant
A ruling obtained by suppression of material facts is void ab initio
An appeal against an AAR ruling lies to the AAAR within 30 days
A ruling binds all taxpayers in the State on the same question
The AAR may decide a question already pending in the applicant's adjudication proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 103 limits the binding effect to the applicant and his jurisdictional officer; section 104 makes a ruling obtained by fraud or suppression void; section 100 allows appeal to the AAAR within 30 days. A ruling does not bind others, and the AAR must reject a question pending or decided in the applicant's proceedings (proviso to section 98(2)).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: an appeal to the High Court under section 117 must be filed within ___ days, and only on a substantial question of law.
questions.explanation: Section 117(2): within 180 days from the date of receipt of the State Bench order, condonable for sufficient cause. The High Court decides only substantial questions of law it formulates.

questions.prompt: Explain the scope, procedure and binding nature of an advance ruling under the CGST Act.
questions.answer:
- **Purpose:** certainty for a proposed or ongoing activity, decided before a dispute arises.
- **Who and what:** any registered person or person seeking registration can apply in ARA-01 with fee, on questions in section 97(2): classification, applicability of notifications, time and value of supply, admissibility of ITC, liability to pay tax, registration, and whether an activity is a supply.
- **Bars:** the AAR shall not admit a question already pending or decided in any proceedings of the applicant.
- **Procedure:** the AAR (one CGST and one SGST member) hears the applicant and the concerned officer and rules within 90 days. A difference between members is referred to the AAAR.
- **Appeal:** to the AAAR by the applicant or the jurisdictional officer within 30 days (plus 30 days); AAAR decides within 90 days.
- **Binding effect (section 103):** only on the applicant and the jurisdictional officer, and only until the law or facts change.
- **Void ruling (section 104):** if obtained by fraud, suppression or misrepresentation, after hearing the applicant.

questions.prompt: Explain liability to pay tax on transfer of business (section 85) and on the death of a person (section 93).
questions.answer:
- **Section 85(1):** where a taxable person transfers his business wholly or partly, by sale, gift, lease, leave and licence, hire or otherwise, the transferor and the transferee are jointly and severally liable for tax, interest or penalty due from the transferor up to the time of transfer, whether determined before or after the transfer.
- **Section 85(2):** the transferee carrying on the business in his own name is liable for tax from the date of transfer and must apply for registration or amendment.
- **Section 93(1)(a):** if a person liable to tax dies and the business is continued by his legal representative or any other person, that person is liable for the tax, interest and penalty due from the deceased.
- **Section 93(1)(b):** if the business is discontinued, the legal representative is liable only to the extent of the estate of the deceased, whether the dues were determined before or after death.
- The idea is that tax dues follow the business and cannot be escaped by a change of ownership.

chapters.title: Customs: Levy, Types of Duties, Classification and Valuation
chapters.summary: Levy under section 12 of the Customs Act, the relevant date for rate and exchange rate, basic customs duty, Social Welfare Surcharge, IGST and trade remedy duties, the General Rules of Interpretation, and valuation of imported goods under the Customs Valuation Rules 2007.
chapters.lawAsOf: Customs Act 1962 and Customs Tariff Act 1975 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Levy, taxable event and relevant dates
lesson.body:
**Section 12 of the Customs Act** levies duty on goods imported into or exported from India at the rates in the **Customs Tariff Act, 1975** (First Schedule: import tariff; Second Schedule: export tariff). Duty also applies to goods belonging to the Government.

**Taxable event:** import is complete when goods cross the customs barrier, that is, when they become part of the mass of goods in India after clearance for home consumption. Export is complete when goods cross the territorial waters of India.

**Rate of duty and tariff value (section 15 for imports, section 16 for exports):**

| Situation | Relevant date |
| --- | --- |
| Goods cleared for home consumption (section 46) | Date the bill of entry is presented, or the date of **entry inwards** of the vessel or arrival of the aircraft, whichever is **later** |
| Goods cleared from a warehouse (section 68) | Date the bill of entry for home consumption (ex-bond) is presented |
| Any other case | Date of payment of duty |
| Export goods | Date of **let export order** |

**Exchange rate (section 14):** the rate notified by CBIC (for imports and for exports separately) in force on the date the **bill of entry is filed** (or shipping bill for exports). Use the CBIC rate, not the RBI rate, in exam problems.

**Exemption (section 25):** the Government can exempt goods generally by notification (absolutely or conditionally) or by special order in exceptional circumstances.

lesson.heading: Types of customs duties
lesson.body:
| Duty | Source | Key point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic customs duty (BCD) | Section 12 CA with First Schedule CTA | Rates in the tariff, often reduced by section 25 notifications |
| Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) | Section 110 of the Finance Act 2018 | **10% of BCD**; some goods exempt |
| Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC) | Finance Act 2021 | On specified goods, often with BCD reduced |
| IGST on imports | Section 3(7) CTA | On assessable value **plus** BCD, SWS and other customs duties; rate as under the IGST Act |
| GST compensation cess | Section 3(9) CTA | Only where still leviable on the goods |
| Protective duty | Section 6 CTA | On Tariff Commission recommendation |
| Safeguard duty | Sections 8B, 8C CTA | Against a sudden surge in imports causing serious injury; up to 4 years, extendable to 10 |
| Countervailing duty on subsidised goods | Section 9 CTA | Equal to the subsidy; up to 5 years, extendable |
| Anti-dumping duty | Section 9A CTA | Up to the **margin of dumping** (normal value minus export price); up to 5 years, extendable |
| Export duty | Second Schedule CTA | Few goods, for example certain ores |

**Import duty format:**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Assessable value (AV) | A |
| BCD at x% of A | B |
| SWS at 10% of B | C |
| Value for IGST = A + B + C (+ anti-dumping or safeguard duty, if any) | D |
| IGST at y% of D | E |
| **Total customs duty = B + C + E** | |

The Finance Act 2026 cut the tariff rate on dutiable goods imported for personal use (heading 9804) to 10%, and moved many effective rates from exemption notifications into the First Schedule.

lesson.heading: Classification: General Rules of Interpretation
lesson.body:
The tariff follows the Harmonized System (HS), with 8-digit tariff items in 21 sections and 98 chapters. Goods are classified using the **General Rules for the Interpretation** (GRI) of the Import Tariff, applied in order:

| Rule | Content |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Titles of sections and chapters are for reference only; classification is by the **terms of the headings** and the **section and chapter notes** |
| 2(a) | An incomplete or unfinished article that has the **essential character** of the complete article is classified as complete; also unassembled or disassembled articles |
| 2(b) | A heading for a material includes mixtures and combinations of it with other materials (then go to rule 3) |
| 3(a) | The heading with the **most specific description** prevails over a general one |
| 3(b) | Mixtures, composite goods and **sets put up for retail sale**: by the material or component that gives the **essential character** |
| 3(c) | If (a) and (b) fail: the heading that occurs **last in numerical order** |
| 4 | Goods that cannot be classified by rules 1 to 3: the heading for goods to which they are **most akin** |
| 5 | Cases for cameras, instruments and similar, shaped for the article and of long use, go with the article; packing goes with the goods unless clearly suitable for repeated use |
| 6 | Subheadings: by their terms and notes, applying rules 1 to 5 at the same level |

**Example:** a hair-cutting set in a leather case containing electric clippers, a comb, scissors and a brush is a set for retail sale; the clippers give it the essential character (rule 3(b)), so the set is classified with electric clippers.

lesson.heading: Valuation of imported goods: section 14 and the 2007 Rules
lesson.body:
Assessable value is the **transaction value**: the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India, for delivery at the time and place of importation, where buyer and seller are not related and price is the sole consideration. The Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 apply.

**Methods in order:** rule 3 (transaction value; related party value accepted if the relationship did not influence the price), rule 4 (identical goods), rule 5 (similar goods), rule 7 (deductive value), rule 8 (computed value; rules 7 and 8 can be reversed at the importer's request), rule 9 (residual). Rule 12 lets the officer reject a declared value where he has reason to doubt its truth, after giving reasons.

**Additions under rule 10(1)**, to the extent borne by the buyer and not already in the price:

- Commission and brokerage, **except buying commission**; cost of containers and packing (labour and materials).
- **Assists** supplied free or at reduced cost by the buyer: materials and components, tools and dies, materials consumed, and engineering, development, artwork, design work, plans and sketches **undertaken elsewhere than in India**.
- Royalties and licence fees related to the goods that the buyer pays **as a condition of sale**.
- Proceeds of any subsequent resale that accrue to the seller.
- Any other payment made as a condition of sale.

**Rule 10(2), cost to the place of importation:**

| Element | If actual cost is not ascertainable |
| --- | --- |
| Cost of transport (freight), including loading, unloading and handling | **20% of FOB value** |
| Insurance | **1.125% of FOB value** |
| Air freight | Actual, but **not more than 20% of FOB value** |

**Worked example.** FOB USD 20,000; freight USD 2,000; insurance not known; buying commission USD 300; CBIC exchange rate ₹86; BCD 10%, SWS 10%, IGST 18%.

| Particulars | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| FOB | USD 20,000 |
| Freight | USD 2,000 |
| Insurance 1.125% of FOB | USD 225 |
| Buying commission | Not added |
| CIF | USD 22,225 |
| **AV at ₹86** | **₹19,11,350** |
| BCD 10% | ₹1,91,135 |
| SWS 10% of BCD | ₹19,114 |
| IGST 18% of ₹21,21,599 | ₹3,81,888 |
| **Total duty** | **₹5,92,136** |

**Common mistakes:** adding buying commission; adding design work done in India; using the RBI rate; computing SWS on AV instead of BCD; and leaving BCD and SWS out of the IGST base.

keyPoints: Section 15: import rate on later of bill of entry date and entry inwards; ex-bond clearance on the ex-bond bill of entry date. Section 16: export rate on let export order date.
Exchange rate: CBIC-notified rate on the date of filing the bill of entry (section 14).
SWS = 10% of BCD. IGST base = AV + BCD + SWS (+ other customs duties). Anti-dumping up to margin of dumping.
GRI order: 1 (headings and notes), 2(a) essential character of incomplete goods, 3(a) specific, 3(b) essential character, 3(c) last numerical, 4 most akin, 5 cases, 6 subheadings.
Rule 10 adds selling commission, packing, assists made outside India, royalty as condition of sale; not buying commission.
Freight unknown: 20% of FOB; insurance unknown: 1.125% of FOB; air freight capped at 20% of FOB.

questions.prompt: Explain the General Rules for the Interpretation of the Import Tariff, with an example of rule 3.
questions.answer:
- **Rule 1:** section and chapter titles are for reference only; classification is by the terms of the headings and the section and chapter notes. Most goods are classified at this step.
- **Rule 2(a):** incomplete or unfinished articles having the essential character of the finished article, and unassembled or disassembled articles, are classified as the complete article. **Rule 2(b):** a reference to a material includes mixtures and combinations with other materials.
- **Rule 3:** where goods are classifiable under two or more headings: (a) the most specific description prevails; (b) mixtures, composite goods and sets for retail sale are classified by the component that gives essential character; (c) otherwise the heading last in numerical order.
- **Rule 4:** goods not classifiable otherwise go under the heading of goods to which they are most akin.
- **Rule 5:** specially shaped cases and containers of long use go with the article; packing goes with the goods unless suitable for repetitive use.
- **Rule 6:** subheadings are classified by their terms and notes, comparing only subheadings at the same level.
- **Example:** a breakfast set of a toaster, a coffee maker and a sandwich maker sold together; if no single item gives essential character, rule 3(c) applies.

questions.prompt: Describe the duties levied on imported goods under the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff Act, including trade remedy duties.
questions.answer:
- **Basic customs duty:** levied by section 12 of the Customs Act at the rates in the First Schedule to the CTA, subject to section 25 exemptions.
- **Social Welfare Surcharge:** 10% of the aggregate customs duties under section 110 of the Finance Act 2018; some goods exempt. **AIDC** on notified goods.
- **IGST (section 3(7) CTA):** at the IGST rate on AV plus BCD, SWS and other customs duties (section 3(8)). **Compensation cess (section 3(9))** where still leviable.
- **Protective duty (section 6):** to protect an Indian industry on Tariff Commission advice.
- **Safeguard duty (section 8B):** where increased imports cause or threaten serious injury to domestic industry; no proof of unfair trade needed; up to 10 years in total.
- **Countervailing duty on subsidised articles (section 9):** up to the amount of subsidy given by the exporting country.
- **Anti-dumping duty (section 9A):** up to the margin of dumping where goods are exported at less than normal value and cause material injury; valid 5 years, extendable after sunset review.
- **Export duty:** on goods in the Second Schedule.

chapters.title: Customs: Procedures, Warehousing, Drawback, Baggage and Refunds
chapters.summary: Import and export procedures, self-assessment and payment of duty, demands under section 28, warehousing under Chapter IX, duty drawback under sections 74 and 75, baggage, and refunds and remissions.
chapters.lawAsOf: Customs Act 1962 as amended by Finance Act 2026; Baggage Rules 2026

lesson.heading: Import and export procedures
lesson.body:
**Import:**

- The carrier files the **Import General Manifest** (IGM, section 30) before the vessel or aircraft arrives. Unloading is allowed only after **entry inwards** (section 31).
- The importer files a **bill of entry** (section 46) electronically, normally in advance of arrival; late filing attracts charges. Three types: for **home consumption**, for **warehousing** (into-bond) and **ex-bond** (clearance from warehouse).
- **Self-assessment (section 17):** the importer assesses duty; the officer may verify, re-assess and pass a speaking order if the importer disagrees.
- **Payment (section 47):** duty is paid by the importer; if not paid by the end of the day (excluding holidays) after the bill of entry is returned for payment, **interest at 15%** per annum runs until payment. Then the officer passes the **out of charge** order for home consumption.

**Export:**

- Exporter files a **shipping bill** (section 50); goods are examined if selected and a **let export order** (section 51) is given. The rate of export duty is the rate on the date of let export order (section 16).
- The carrier files the **Export General Manifest** (section 41).

**Demand of duty (section 28):**

| Case | Time limit for SCN from relevant date | Paid before SCN | Paid within 30 days of SCN |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Non-fraud (28(1)) | 2 years | Duty + interest; no penalty and no SCN | Proceedings concluded on payment of duty and interest |
| Fraud, collusion, wilful misstatement, suppression (28(4)) | 5 years | Duty + interest + **15%** penalty | Duty + interest + **25%** penalty |

Interest on delayed duty is payable under section 28AA. Where an order confirms a fraud demand, penalty under section 114A equals the duty, reduced to **25%** if duty, interest and penalty are paid within 30 days of the order.

lesson.heading: Warehousing: sections 57 to 73A
lesson.body:
Warehousing lets an importer defer duty until goods are cleared, or avoid it if they are re-exported.

| Point | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| Types | Public warehouse (57), private warehouse (58), special warehouse for notified goods under customs control (58A) |
| Bond | Importer executes a bond for **three times the duty** assessed (section 59) |
| Order | Proper officer passes a warehousing order (section 60); goods are deemed cleared from the customs station |
| Period (section 61) | Capital goods for EOU, EHTP, STP and similar units: until cleared. Other goods for such units: until consumed or cleared. **Any other goods: 1 year** from the warehousing order, extendable |
| Manufacture in bond (section 65) | Manufacturing and other operations in the warehouse with permission; duty deferred; nil duty if the product is exported |
| Clearance for home consumption (section 68) | Ex-bond bill of entry and payment of duty, interest and charges |
| Export from warehouse (section 69) | No import duty if the goods are exported |
| Goods not cleared in time (section 72) | Officer demands the full duty, interest and penalties and can sell the goods |

**Rate and value on ex-bond clearance:** rate of duty is the rate on the date the **ex-bond bill of entry** is presented (section 15(1)(b)); the value and exchange rate are those determined when the **into-bond bill of entry** was filed.

**Worked example.** Goods with AV ₹20,00,000 are warehoused when BCD is 10%. They are cleared ex-bond after BCD falls to 7.5%. Duty = BCD 1,50,000 + SWS 15,000 + IGST 18% of 21,65,000 (3,89,700) = **₹5,54,700**.

lesson.heading: Duty drawback: sections 74 and 75
lesson.body:
**Section 74, re-export of imported goods:**

- Goods on which import duty was paid are re-exported, identified to the satisfaction of the officer, within **2 years** from the date of payment of duty (extendable by the Board).
- **Not used** after import: **98%** of the import duty paid.
- **Used** after import: a reduced percentage by period of use, under the Re-export of Imported Goods (Drawback of Customs Duties) Rules, 1995.

**Section 75, drawback on imported materials used in manufacture of export goods:**

- Compensates customs duty (and specified other duties) paid on inputs used in making export goods, under the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017.
- **All Industry Rates** (AIR) are notified as a percentage of FOB, sometimes with a per-unit cap.
- **Brand rate** is fixed for an individual exporter on application where AIR is not available or is less than 80% of actual duties suffered.
- No drawback where the value of the export goods is less than the value of imported materials used in them (negative value addition), or where sale proceeds are not realised in time under FEMA.

Drawback is paid along with interest if it is not paid within 1 month of the claim (section 75A), and the exporter repays it with interest if export proceeds are not realised.

lesson.heading: Baggage, refunds and remissions
lesson.body:
**Baggage (sections 77 to 81):** the passenger declares the contents of baggage to the proper officer (section 77). Bona fide baggage is classified under heading 9803 and charged at the tariff rate, after the free allowance. The **Baggage Rules, 2026** replaced the 2016 Rules from February 2026 and raised the general free allowance for passengers arriving other than by land to **₹75,000**, besides used personal effects. Unaccompanied baggage can be cleared within the prescribed period.

**Refund (section 27):** an application must be made within **1 year** from the date of payment of duty or interest. The doctrine of **unjust enrichment** applies: refund is credited to the **Consumer Welfare Fund** unless the applicant proves that the incidence of duty was not passed on. Refund due to an appellate order is paid without fresh application. Minimum refund ₹100. **Section 27A:** interest at 6% if not refunded within 3 months.

**Remission and abatement:**

| Section | Situation | Relief |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13 | Goods pilfered after unloading and before the order for clearance or warehousing | No duty on pilfered goods (the custodian is liable) |
| 22 | Goods damaged or deteriorated before or during unloading, or before examination | Duty abated in proportion to loss of value |
| 23 | Goods lost or destroyed before clearance; or goods relinquished before clearance | Remission of duty |

**Common mistakes:** using the into-bond date for the rate on ex-bond clearance; giving 98% drawback on used goods; ignoring the 15% penalty on fraud cases paid before SCN; and refunding to the importer without testing unjust enrichment.

keyPoints: Bill of entry types: home consumption, warehousing (into-bond), ex-bond. Interest at 15% on delayed payment of duty (section 47).
Section 28: SCN within 2 years (non-fraud) or 5 years (fraud). Fraud paid before SCN: 15% penalty; within 30 days of SCN: 25%. Section 114A: 25% if paid within 30 days of the order.
Warehousing bond: 3 times duty. Period for normal goods: 1 year. Rate on ex-bond date; value and exchange rate on into-bond date.
Section 74: re-export within 2 years; unused goods get 98% of duty.
Section 75: AIR or brand rate (when AIR is below 80% of duties suffered); no drawback on negative value addition.
Section 27 refund within 1 year; unjust enrichment, Consumer Welfare Fund; 6% interest after 3 months.

cases.title: Case: Arora Polymers Ltd
cases.body:
Arora Polymers Ltd, a manufacturer in the domestic tariff area (not an EOU), has these customs matters in 2027:

- **Warehousing:** it warehoused a consignment of polymer resin in a public warehouse under a warehousing order dated 1 March 2027.
- **Defective machine:** it paid import duty of ₹6,00,000 on a moulding machine on 15 January 2027. The machine was found defective, was never used, and was re-exported to the supplier on 10 June 2027 after the officer identified it.
- **Excess duty:** on 10 January 2027 it paid ₹1,20,000 of excess duty because of a classification error. It has already sold the finished goods, and its cost sheets show the duty was included in their price.

questions.prompt: An importer wants to store goods in a customs warehouse instead of clearing them for home consumption. Which document does he file?
options: Bill of entry for home consumption
Bill of entry for warehousing (into-bond)
Ex-bond bill of entry
Shipping bill
questions.explanation: Section 46 allows a bill of entry for home consumption or for warehousing. The into-bond bill of entry is used to deposit goods in a warehouse; the ex-bond bill of entry is filed later when they are cleared for home consumption.

questions.prompt: Duty was short-levied because the importer wilfully misdeclared the goods. Within what period from the relevant date can a show cause notice be issued?
options: 1 year
2 years
3 years
5 years
questions.explanation: Section 28(4): in cases of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, the SCN can be issued within 5 years from the relevant date. Non-fraud cases under section 28(1) have 2 years.

questions.prompt: Until when can Arora keep the polymer resin in the warehouse without an extension?
options: Until 29 May 2027 (90 days)
Until 29 February 2028 (1 year)
Until cleared, with no limit
Until 1 March 2030 (3 years)
questions.explanation: Section 61(1)(c): goods other than those for EOUs and similar units may stay until the expiry of 1 year from the warehousing order, extendable by the Commissioner. From 1 March 2027 that runs to 29 February 2028 (2028 is a leap year).

questions.prompt: Arora files a refund claim for the excess duty of ₹1,20,000 on 5 December 2027. What is the likely outcome?
options: Refund paid to Arora with 6% interest
Claim rejected as time-barred
Refund sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund, because the duty was passed on
Refund paid to the buyers of the finished goods automatically
questions.explanation: The claim is within 1 year of payment (10 January 2027), so it is in time under section 27. But the duty was included in the price of goods sold, so the incidence was passed on. Under the unjust enrichment rule, the amount is credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund.

questions.prompt: Drawback under section 74 on re-export of imported goods is available only if the goods are re-exported within 2 years from the date of payment of import duty, unless the Board extends the period.
questions.explanation: Section 74(1) requires re-export within 2 years from the date of payment of duty on import; the Board can extend the period for sufficient cause. The goods must also be identified to the satisfaction of the officer.

questions.prompt: In which situations does the Customs Act give relief from duty (no duty, abatement or remission)?
options: Goods pilfered after unloading and before the order for clearance
Goods damaged during unloading in the port
Goods lost or destroyed before clearance for home consumption
Goods relinquished by the importer before the order for clearance
Goods stolen from the importer's factory after clearance
questions.explanation: Section 13 (pilferage before clearance order), section 22 (damage before or during unloading) and section 23 (loss, destruction or relinquishment before clearance) give relief. Once goods are cleared for home consumption, duty is final and theft afterwards gives no relief.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a refund claim under section 27 of the Customs Act must be filed within ___ year(s) from the date of payment of duty.
questions.explanation: Section 27(1): within 1 year from the date of payment of duty or interest. The limit does not apply to duty paid under protest; the date of payment is then the date the protest is resolved.

questions.prompt: Compute the total customs duty payable on clearance of the goods from the warehouse (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: Goods were warehoused on an into-bond bill of entry when BCD was 10%. Their assessable value, determined at that time, is ₹20,00,000. They are cleared for home consumption on an ex-bond bill of entry after BCD is reduced to 7.5%. SWS 10% of BCD; IGST 18% throughout. Ignore interest.
questions.explanation:
Section 15(1)(b): the rate in force on the date the ex-bond bill of entry is presented applies. Value was fixed at the into-bond stage.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Assessable value | 20,00,000 |
| BCD 7.5% | 1,50,000 |
| SWS 10% of BCD | 15,000 |
| IGST 18% of 21,65,000 | 3,89,700 |
| **Total duty** | **5,54,700** |

questions.prompt: Compute the interest payable under section 47 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.data: Duty of ₹4,00,000 on a bill of entry for home consumption was paid 10 days after the last day allowed for payment. Interest rate notified: 15% per annum.

questions.prompt: Compute the drawback Arora can claim on re-export of the defective moulding machine (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.explanation:
The machine was re-exported within 2 years of paying duty, was identified, and was never used. Section 74 gives 98% of the import duty.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Import duty paid | 6,00,000 |
| **Drawback 98%** | **5,88,000** |

questions.prompt: Under section 16, which date's rate of export duty applies to goods exported by sea?
options: Date the shipping bill is filed
Date of the let export order
Date the vessel leaves Indian territorial waters
Date the export proceeds are realised
questions.explanation: Section 16(1)(a): for goods entered for export under section 50, the rate and tariff value in force on the date the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading (let export order) apply.

questions.prompt: Compute the amount payable in each case and state whether a show cause notice will be issued.
questions.data:
During a post-clearance audit, two short levies are found for an importer.

| Case | Nature | Short-levied duty (₹) | Interest up to payment (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Wrong rate applied by mistake, no intent | 3,00,000 | 27,000 |
| B | Wilful undervaluation | 5,00,000 | 90,000 |

The importer pays both before any SCN. Also show the amount for case B if it is paid within 30 days of the SCN (assume interest is the same).
questions.answer:
| Case | Provision | Duty (₹) | Interest (₹) | Penalty (₹) | Total (₹) | SCN? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A, paid before SCN | 28(2) | 3,00,000 | 27,000 | Nil | 3,27,000 | No SCN for the amount paid |
| B, paid before SCN | 28(5): 15% of duty | 5,00,000 | 90,000 | 75,000 | 6,65,000 | Officer may issue SCN only for any short payment |
| B, paid within 30 days of SCN | 28(6): 25% of duty | 5,00,000 | 90,000 | 1,25,000 | 7,15,000 | Proceedings deemed concluded |

Time limits: SCN within 2 years (case A) and 5 years (case B) from the relevant date. If case B goes to adjudication, penalty under section 114A equals the duty, reduced to 25% if paid within 30 days of the order.

questions.prompt: Explain the main provisions on warehousing of imported goods under Chapter IX of the Customs Act.
questions.answer:
- **Licensing:** public warehouses (section 57) and private warehouses (section 58) are licensed by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; special warehouses (section 58A) hold notified goods under physical customs control.
- **Deposit:** the importer files an into-bond bill of entry, executes a bond for three times the duty (section 59), and the officer passes a warehousing order (section 60); goods are then deemed to have left the customs station.
- **Period (section 61):** capital goods for EOU and similar units: until cleared; other goods for them: until consumed or cleared; any other goods: 1 year from the warehousing order, extendable.
- **Operations:** owner can inspect, sort and repack (section 64); manufacture and other operations in bond with permission (section 65).
- **Removal:** clearance for home consumption on payment of duty (section 68), at the rate on the ex-bond bill of entry date; export without payment of duty (section 69); transfer to another warehouse (section 67).
- **Default (section 72):** if goods are not removed in time or are removed improperly, the officer demands full duty with interest and penalty and can detain and sell the goods.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between drawback under section 74 and drawback under section 75 of the Customs Act.
questions.answer:
| Point | Section 74 | Section 75 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goods exported | Imported goods re-exported as such (used or unused) | Goods manufactured in India using imported materials |
| Duty refunded | Import duty paid on the same goods | Duty on imported inputs used in the export product, under the Drawback Rules 2017 |
| Rate | 98% if unused; reduced rates by period of use if used | All Industry Rate as % of FOB, or brand rate for the exporter |
| Time | Re-export within 2 years of duty payment | Linked to export; proceeds to be realised under FEMA |
| Identity | Goods must be identified | No identity test; standard input norms |

Both carry interest if drawback is not paid within 1 month of the claim (section 75A), and section 75 drawback is recovered if export proceeds are not realised.
